A quadrupedal robot's ability to move efficiently and adaptively is heavily dependent on its ability to navigate diverse terrain environments. Traditional learning methods may struggle to generalize across different environments due to their preconditions, requiring multiple rewards schemes that are often not easily defined. Evolving the reward function further complicates the matter, leading to inefficient optimization. We introduce the EPG framework, a method that uses an evolutionary algorithm to develop a universal terrain representation, bypassing the need for manual reward function definition or evolutionary optimization. In this framework, the EPG represents the agent's movement as a series of pose positions in a gene pool and leverages an evolutionary optimizer to develop a universal terrain representation. This approach is highly effective when combined with a dispatch policy that selects the most suitable pose positions based on the evolved terrain representation. Experimental results show that the EPG achieves adaptive and efficient quadrupedal locomotion across diverse environments while reducing the data required for learning and adapting to new situations. The mechanism of the EPG also enables the control of complex and diverse robots through a single evolved pathway. Additionally, the dispatch policy allows the control of multiple quadrupedal robots in the same environment through a optimized pathway, revealing the potential of the EPG to be a general approach to learning control policies. Furthermore, the success of the EPG quadrupedal control has been replicated on a hexapod robot, demonstrating its general applicability to diverse robot configurations. The introduction of the EPG framework represents a groundbreaking approach to developing adaptive and efficient control policies for a wide range of robot configurations, revolutionizing the field of reinforcement learning and robotic control. The code for the EPG framework is publicly available at the following repository: https://github.com/RobotLearning/EvolvingPathwayGenerator. The videos showcasing the EPG quadrupedal and hexapod robots in action are available at the following links: https://robotlearning.github.io/video/quad.html and https://robotlearning.githubio/video/hexapod.html. Identifying anomalies in real-time streaming data is particularly challenging due to their unpredictability, rapid occurrence, and continuous flow. Current anomaly detection approaches are largely confined to structured data and struggle with the diversity of streaming data formats, or with large datasets and complex anomalies. We present ReAD, a framework for detecting local anomalies in streaming data streams, especially linear trajectories. ReAD divides the trajectory map into smaller areas using a dynamic partitioning method and assigns a weight to each area based on the trajectories within it, thus effectively detecting anomalies. Our approach is accompanied by extensive performance assessments and comparisons with the existing state-of-the-art methodologies. The results show that ReAD outperforms the competing methods in precision, recall, and F1-score by significant margins. Moreover, the external evaluations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed technique. The implementation details and test data are available for reproduction, hosted at https://github.com/JiashuKang/ReAD. Evaluation experiments reveal a ~3 times acceleration in execution speed with the loss of only a minor decrease in performance. The performance of ReAD is most affected by the parameter $N$ followed by $T$ and ${\theta}_{{max}}$, in descending order. Future developments of the framework could be enriched by incorporating more robust distance metrics and support for other types of anomalies. Considering its superiority, we propose ReAD as a premier method for detecting local anomalies in real-time streaming data. The superiority of ReAD is confirmed despite its relatively simple design and limited complexity. The efficacy of ReAD is attributed to its effectiveness in dividing linear trajectories into smaller areas for anomaly detection and weighting them based on the trajectories within the areas. This discerning ability, coupled with its efficiency in the partitioning and weighting processes, sets ReAD apart from the competing methods. The superiority of ReAD is evident across various benchmarks and evaluation scenarios, signifying its potential as a trusted tool for processing and analyzing streaming data streams. The proposed framework provides significant value in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score, thus contributing to the development of novel techniques in the category. The contribution of ReAD is two-fold, consisting of the method and the benchmark. The method, marked by efficiency and effectiveness, is well-suited for supporting research in the area. The benchmark, created to simulate real-world applications, enables thorough evaluations and offers a standardized methodology for comparing the performance of local anomaly detection algorithms. Consequently, the proposed framework and benchmark will facilitate the development and analysis of streaming data detection algorithms based on specific requirements and evaluation criteria.

By applying advanced semantics and logic, this method enables comparisons across different programming languages and identifies common elements of program meaning. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we analyze DWIFOB's convergence and efficiency. Our findings indicate that DWIFOB has stronger convergence properties than the forward-backward algorithm, and it also outperforms other acceleration strategies when available. Furthermore, we provide numerical experiments that demonstrate the advantages of DWIFOB. To a great extent, DWIFOB generalizes the forward-backward algorithm, and it offers an effective solution to monotone inclusion problems that cannot be solved through proximal methods. However, DWIFOB may not be applicable in cases where the operators involved are not positively defined, which is a crucial requirement for its operation. An improved variant of DWIFOB, referred to as ifobbled DWIFOB (iDWIFOB), is designed to address this limitation and is applicable even when operators are only monotone. Interestingly, iDWIFOB performs similarly to DWIFOB in experiments involving positively defined operators, and it also outperforms other acceleration methods in tasks involving non-positive and monotone operators. Through this approach, we provide concrete evidence that accelerating forward-backward algorithms can yield better results, which is an observation previously noted empirically in the literature. The insulating characteristics were confirmed by partial density of states analysis and are attributed to the disruption of electron flow caused by twisted and anisotropically deformed chemical bonds. The presence of Te$p_x$ and Tl$6s$ orbital components in the valence band tops further indicates enhanced chemical bonding between Te and Tl ions. Both materials displayed robust stability through the constant pressure finite strain method, with a very small compressive strain of -0.035 GPa/fu at equilibrium. The optimal layer stacking configuration in MTl$_4$Te$_3$ was found to be hexagonal, accordant with experimental XRD observations, and both materials exhibited excellent chemical stability when compared to other teletellurides. The exceptional properties of large band gap MTl$_4$Te$_3$ topological insulators make them promising candidates for a range of advanced solid-state devices. The calculated values of elastic constants for MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (Cd, Hg) with a hexagonal stack configuration also displayed close proximity to the magic angle condition, with a small deviation of 0.041° (Cd) and 0.048° (Hg). This means that MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) with a hexagonal stack configuration possesses robust insulating and elastic properties. We investigate the platform groups of iterates of bicritical rational functions, focusing initial examination on those of degree two. The platform group of an iterate is a subgroup of the full Galois group by definition. We establish criteria to identify when the platform group and Galois group are equal, specifically for bicritical functions of degree two with distinct irreducible polynomials in a finite field. The conditions revolve around the symmetry of a polynomial's conjugacy class, particularly its cycle structure in a specific base and the presence or absence of fixed points within that base. Notably, we highlight an exceptional case where the platform group and Galois group differ, specifically for $f(x) = (1+x^2)^{1/2} + (1+x^2)^{1/2}$, an iterate of which has a Galois group of order 16. We further explore properties of its Galois group, including its action on the ramification set and its cycle structure in various cases. Utilizing twistor theory, we demonstrate that the Galois group acts triply on the ramification set and show cycle structures for most bicritical polynomials of degree two with distinct irreducible polynomials, except for three specific families, which we identify and discuss. The action of the Galois group on the ramification set is found to be highly regular in most cases, with exceptional patterns observed for polynomials of the form $x^2 + a^2$ and $x^2 + a^2z^2 + b^2z^4$ for $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}, a>0, b>0$. We show that the Galois group of $f(x)^2 + 1$ has order 16 if $a=1, b=1$, while it is unknown for other cases. Additionally, we conclude with an open question regarding whether the Galois group of $x^2 + z^2 + tz$ has a highly regular action on the ramification set for any $t \in \mathbb{Q}, t>1$. We provide supporting numerical evidence and observations for this specific scenario. Finally, we offer several general open questions and hypotheses related to the Galois groups of iterates, particularly for those of degree two, which we pose for consideration. Notably, we propose the hypothesis that the Galois group of $f(x)^2 + 1$ is a member of the family $A4, A3, A2 or S3$

Utilizing an approach that blends these three quantities with the eta-eta prime mixing parameter Neta, we derive constraints for the quarkmass differences and the eta prime mass by incorporating experimental values of the eta prime decay widths into the formula etap = sqrt(mu_s^2 + (Neta * eta - mu_s)^2). This results in the quarkmass differences eta - etap = 0.0037 GeV and eta' - u_s^2 = 0.0303 GeV^2, which aligns with numerous other calculations, including those obtained through lattice QCD, quasivariational approach, and SU(3) flavor symmetry constraints. We also report the eta prime mass at zero quarkmass difference as 1.0034 GeV. Furthermore, our findings for the quarkmass differences align with numerous other calculations, whereas the etap mass at zero quarkmass difference differs from the current lattice QCD calculations. By analyzing 1.8 million GitHub repositories, we found that 83% of them are clones of existing repositories on the platform, and a significant proportion of these cloned repositories receive updates. High-stakes scientific and engineering fields such as physics and aerospace engineering often involve making critical predictions based on data, which must be accompanied by reliable estimates of uncertainty. However, the process of sampling these fields frequently yields contaminated data, which may contain abnormal and unrepresentative values. Such data, susceptible to manipulation by malicious parties, can severely undermine the accuracy of future predictions and operational decisions if not detected and rectified. Given that existing methods for identifying and correcting contaminated data are relatively basic and vulnerable to flaws, we develop more effective strategies for detecting and mitigating the influence of corrupted data on least squares estimation. These strategies, which do not dismiss entire datasets, instead weigh each sample according to its credibility. Our approach to determining confidence weights involves a combination of a randomization technique and an advanced optimization method, which enables us to quantify the amount of damage that could result from a certain level of corruption. Through theoretical and numerical analysis, we assess the robustness of this approach and use it to create reliable models of unmanageable real-world systems, such as a crowd-counting app that must operate in the presence of surveillance camera interference. Ultimately, this framework enables us to make more accurate predictions and guarantee the quality of our outcomes, even when operating in noisy environments. We develop a novel framework to incorporate human feedback in reinforcement learning when some aspects of an agent's policy are already approved. Traditional inverse reinforcement learning widely assumes unregulated environments, whereas in real-world scenarios, agents often benefit from partial human feedback indicating what actions are correct. Existing methods either neglect human input or treat all feedback equally, despite varying levels of certainty associated with each hint. To address these shortcomings, our framework organizes human feedback into a probabilistic model that translates partial hints into a fully detailed action policy. This framework is comprised of three key components: first, human feedback is filtered to exclude actions conflicting with available rewards and constraints; second, the remaining feedback is incorporated into a probabilistic model that estimates an agent's utility function; finally, our approach optimizes a maximal entropy policy compatible with both human input and regulatory rewards. To facilitate the agent's decision-making, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution of an infinite mixture model using a hierarchical Bayesian model combining gamma and beta distributions. Through theoretical and practical validation, our approach outperforms existing methods in various test cases, including a 2D navigation task and a self-driving car simulation. Crucially, our framework enables agents to learn from multiple human contributors with diverse perspectives, effectively incorporating diverse hints into an agent's policy. Lastly, our approach is versatile and adaptable to various scenarios, including the emergence of new hints and the update of existing knowledge. This work examines the robustness of small loop transfer regions for linear control systems when the system matrix contains uncertainties from a vector $\Delta H$. We define a set of polyhedral boundaries resulting from the discrete model of the small loop transfer problem, and our analysis shows that these boundaries robustly contain the actual transfer region under certain conditions on $\Delta H$. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, this method's implications for parameter-dependent Lyapunov functions and robust small-gain theorems in control systems are discussed. We also provide a geometric interpretation of our transfer regions, along with a demonstration of tightly enclosing these regions, although this remains an open issue. The proposed transfer region bound is shown to be more accurate in certain scenarios than a standard bounding method. Furthermore, we investigated the structural properties of the system matrix $H(\Delta x, \Delta \nu)$, which describes a class of controlled polytopes, and we define a type of locally finite boundary that encloses the fundamental group of a controlled polytope without relying on its specific realization. We then develop an algorithm to generate this type of boundary with an arbitrarily small diameter. Finally, we studied the relationship between the small loop transfer region and this enclosing boundary, and we investigate its validity in general. However, we observed that this encapsulation may not hold for all classes of control, particularly in a case study involving a parameter-dependent control class. Therefore, we propose an alternative type of boundary that is uniquely associated with the fundamental group of a controlled polytope and serves as a valid enclosing boundary, and we provide a verification algorithm for its effectiveness. Furthermore, we extend our methods and theories to the realm of smooth loops, which leads to novel contributions and research questions in this area. We also provide a demonstration of our theoretical results through numerical examples and open issues for future research. Given the independence of our approaches, this work can serve as a comprehensive guide to analyzing small loop transfer regions, as well as providing valuable tools for practical applications in control systems. This study is the second in a series focusing on the mass distribution of black holes across various cosmic ages, with the first series predicting the emergence of intermediate-mass black holes through a continuous process from seed stars' remains. For this second series, researchers consider two initial conditions for black hole creation: star explosions that leave behind extremely large black holes and pre-existing large black holes resulting from earlier star formations. Either of these scenarios leads to a higher-than-expected number of massive black holes compared to traditional theories, with substantial implications for their overall mass and luminosity distribution. With the possibility of these massive black hole origins, it's plausible that ultra-low frequency gravitational wave detectors like LISA will identify a broader spectrum of massive black holes, and that these devices will primarily detect the vibrations of large, ancient black holes. Furthermore, this leads to the prediction that the brightest electromagnetic sources associated with these massive black holes are typically found near the center of large galaxies. As a result, these bright sources may be more often discovered in the centers of these galaxies. Additionally, this leads to the prediction that the less explosive supernovae associated with the remaining massive black hole seeds may be more often linked to unusual, extremely distant galaxy structures and, further, that these massive black holes may be more often found at the centers of these galaxies. Lastly, these predictions indicate that these massive black holes are more often discovered in very large galaxies and, further, that their growth through mergers of smaller black holes may not be sufficient to explain their entire mass when considering their overall age and star formation patterns in these galaxies. In contrast, this leads to the alternative prediction that the continuous process of merging with less massive black holes over their entire history may be more often sufficient to explain the entire mass of these massive black holes. In summary, these results indicate that the origin of massive black holes may lead to broader, less predictable patterns in their overall mass distribution compared to traditional theories, and further highlight the need for more flexible and unpredictable models in black hole creation in order to fully explain their entire mass spectrum. As a result, this leads to the predictions that massive black hole detection and study may require a broader range of search strategies and considerations, and further that their unique behaviors and occurrences may provide valuable insights into the entire history of cosmic mass formation. This paper introduces several innovative solutions to support researchers in keeping an electronic journal, focusing on ease of use and adaptable solutions that can be tailored to diverse research settings. We present two primary approaches: (1) the relocation of existing tools to provide a unified digital space for research data and (2) introducing fundamental software functionality to facilitate seamless research workflow integration. Ultimately, our aim is to provide scientists with easy-to-use digital tools to enhance their research workflow, similar to how laboratory scientists benefit from standard laboratory equipment. 

Digital tools now offer various functions to support research activities, such as data management, collaboration management, and information search and retrieval. However, many of these tools were initially intended for other purposes, and researchers may not benefit equally from their functionality. This paper presents several innovative solutions to enhance research productivity by modifying existing digital tools, combining them to meet specific research demands, and making them accessible to researchers. We demonstrate the utility of these solutions in an example from the Linzer Geographisch-Historisches Labyrinth.

The $T$ matrix is modeled as an $T_{cc}^+$ state composed of three constituent quarks in a high-spin configuration and features flavor-changing neutral currents. The decay width of around 15 MeV is found to be in agreement with experimental observations. The study also indicates that most of the decay width is allocated to the dipole form factor in the direction perpendicular to the plane containing the $D^{\ast}$ and $D$ mesons. The calculated branching fractions show that the dominant decay modes of the $T_{cc}^+$ are primarily to the $D^{\ast} D$ and $D D\pi$ pairs, with the former accounting for around 98% of the total decay width. The predicted partial decay width for $T_{cc}^+$ decaying into $D^{\ast}D\pi$ through the flavor-changing neutral current in a high-spin configuration is in agreement with a recent estimate by the same authors. The study further reveals that higher-order corrections to the decay width of around 10 MeV can be anticipated due to mechanisms such as loop and soft-glueball contributions. The investigation also indicates that certain non-relativistic corrections to the decay width, arising from interactions between the constituent quarks, can be significant. The study also explores potential effects from glueball components in the $T$-matrix structure, which could result in detectable differences in decay properties, particularly those involving decay modes sensitive to alignment, that may be observable in future experiments. The investigation also indicates that light glueball components are likely to be visible in future experiments with high-proton beams. The study further estimates that direct production of the $T_{cc}^+$ through flavor-changing neutral currents would result in a yield below the threshold of 100 $T_{cc}^+$ events at the HL-LHC. The investigation also indicates that light $T$-matrix resonances may be more suitable for production and study in experiments using high-proton beams due to their potential for observed resonant signals. Researchers previously developed an efficient method to calculate the nonlinearity of vector-based Boolean functions, which we extend to a higher dimension scenario. Relying on properties of Slim Sidon sets, we determine nonlinearity values for certain key functions, specifically those from $\mathbb{F}_{2^k}^n$ to $\mathbbak{F}_{2^k}^m$ with specific characteristics. These results lead to unique insights into Slim Sidon sets and offer new perspectives on their properties. Furthermore, our work enables us to identify optimal vector-based Boolean functions in certain constraint systems and provides us with approximations for a hypothesis related to Slim Sidon sets and its implications in combinatorics. Additionally, our research may have implications in architecture and design for cryptographic primitives such as permutation polynomials and hash functions. We also discover a connection between Slim Sidon sets and a type of multivariate polynomial system known as the ARS system, which has far-reaching applications in areas such as coding theory and cryptography. We present an efficient method to calculate the nonlinearity of vector-based Boolean functions, which can be used to solve multivariate polynomial systems under specific conditions. These results provide new directions for research in property preserving transformations, which have significant practical applications in areas such as intrusion detection and biometric authentication. Finally, our work may lead to new insights in the area of signal design due to its low energy properties. The nonlinearity values we determine can also be applied to evaluate a vector-based function's resistance to linear attacks and side-channel analyses. We also derive lower and upper bounds for a related metric known as the semi-linear nonlinearity and provide direct and indirect proofs for several related hypotheses and open problems. Furthermore, our work may have implications in areas such as coding theory and cryptography due to its broad applications and the related systems it can be applied to. The nonlinearity values we present can also be utilized to evaluate a vector-based function's resistance to various types of attacks, which has significant practical applications and offers new directions for research in areas such as permutation polynomials, hash functions, intrusion detection, biometric authentication and signal design. We also offer an efficient method to calculate a related metric known as the semi-linear nonlinearity and provide new insights into Slim Sidon sets and its related systems, which have significant implications in areas such as coding theory and cryptography.

Non-uniform binarization is a method of converting real matrices into binary representations by selecting rows with varying weights, rather than equally. This approach aims to reduce the memory requirements of storing binary data by minimizing the number of rows. To achieve this, modifying the columns of the real matrix by scaling or setting them to zero is essential. However, determining the optimal transformation procedure is complicated due to the non-convex nature of the problem. In this research, a simple and efficient sampling process called SampleM is proposed to approximately achieve low-rank binary conversions of large matrices with fixed margins. SampleM is a column-modified binarization technique that uses a straightforward procedure to select and scale matrix columns. It provides high quality conversions that closely match the optimal binary rank. Experiment results demonstrate that SampleM outperforms existing methods in preserving the structural properties of datasets. The algorithm is particularly effective for large-scale matrix conversion tasks and has been successfully applied in data compression and synthetic dataset generation. Our technique for generating optical frequency combs in microresonators employs a single pump laser to create a stable and reproducible comb pattern, enabling easy alignment and adjusting the spacing between combs. By adjusting the pump power, the researcher can select the desired level of spectral extension and precision, depending on the microresonator and optical conditions. This versatile approach may facilitate generating multi-channel coherent light for applications such as spectroscopy, metrology, and telecommunications. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness using a specific microresonator and generate combs with 1 nm, 5 nm, and 13 nm spacing, covering areas up to 250 GHz. Our parametric sowing technique allows microcomb generation to be implemented in various applications where a limited range of combs are required. It also provides a pathway for adjusting comb parameters to accommodate changing conditions in repeater networks for fiber-optic communications. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to decrease storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats binary weights as stochastic random variables under rounding uncertainty and analyzes their distribution during training. We derive the neural tangent kernel for binary weight architectures, revealing that increased variance in the weights' representation is correlated with improved generalization. Experimental findings on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 support this theory, and suggest that the beneficial effect of quantization on the neural tangent kernel contributes to its ability to enhance model generalization. Additionally, we propose a post-training evaluation metric to predict the effect of binary weight quantization on generalization performance. These contributions provide a theoretical foundation for the practice of neural quantization and motivate the development of new quantization methods that prioritize generalization. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jaitlne/quantization. We also released binary neural networks pre-trained using our proposed metric at https://jaitlne.github.io/binary-nn. These pre-trained models can be used as a starting point for post-training and deployment processes that prioritize both inference efficiency and generalization. From now on, we will refer to neural networks that prioritize training efficiency as "binary networks" and those that prioritize generalization as "binary models". Similarly, we will use the terms "quantization" and "binaryization" to describe the processes that reduce the storage and processing requirements during inference. Furthermore, we will refer to "neural quantization methods" as techniques that strive to find binary models that strike an optimal balance between generalization and inference efficiency. We provide theoretical foundations for these new concepts through the lens of the neural tangent kernel, specifically by analyzing their effect on the kernel's variance. We empirically verify their effectiveness, and as a result, we can revisit and revise previous studies on neural quantization. Verifying the accurate results of quantum computations is a pressing issue, particularly as the complexity of quantum algorithms increases. We've developed a novel approach using classical computers to verify the outcomes of quantum computations efficiently, even when they're highly complex. This method runs in linear time, requiring only a single pass through the data, whereas previous methods took cubic time. This breakthrough stems from a novel observation regarding the overlap of quantum computation and verification processes, and from applying two fundamental data manipulation techniques, namely, grouping and scanning, to quantum computations. This insight and technique enable us to reduce the complexity of verification by a significant order. We've formally described and proved the correctness of this efficient verification algorithm using a formal specification, and through practical experiments, have found that it outperforms existing methods, often significantly so, even when the complexity of quantum algorithms is low. Furthermore, we've outlined how this efficient verification algorithm can be extended to detect and correct errors in quantum computations accurately. This work presents the first efficient algorithm using classical computers for verifying and correcting errors in quantum computations. We've also established a relationship between the efficiency of verification and detection/correction processes, and formally defined and proved the correctness of this error detection and correction algorithm. Additionally, we've presented criteria for achieving optimal performance in these processes, and have presented a design framework that allows us to create efficient algorithms for a wide range of context-free quantum data using a form of regular expressions, and further, extendable to various types of quantum data. This framework has been thoroughly tested and validated through numerous practical experiments, and has been found to be very effective, often significantly so, in enhancing the efficiency of verification and error detection/correction processes. This work presents the first general solution for efficiently verifying and correcting errors in quantum computations, and has successfully applied these solutions to diverse types of quantum data, and has demonstrated optimality in efficiency for a wide range of applications. Cells in organisms play a vital role in life and their structures serve as a foundation for better comprehension of life processes. However, current cell segmentation and 3D surface reconstruction techniques are not well-suited for analyzing cell shapes due to their simplicity and limited scope. Unlike existing methods, this study utilizes a more comprehensive neural network to generate complete cell surfaces from simplified geometric models, thereby enabling more accurate representation and visualization of cells. Furthermore, this approach enables the generation of synthetic cells, allowing for more effective learning of cellular shape patterns. Using a novel combination of Cycle Consistency and Pairwise Consistency loss functions, this method enables the creation of novel cell shapes based on observed data, thereby enhancing generative modeling of living cells. Our innovative method was evaluated using the FSDC dataset containing human corneal epithelial cell images, which it used to generate complete cell surfaces and create new cell shapes. Our results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over state-of-the-art models in surface reconstruction and image synthesis tasks. Furthermore, the generated cell shapes were found to closely resemble real cell shapes and the method was found to closely replicate the original cell surfaces during inference. In recent years, researchers have utilized reinforcement learning's capabilities to map an irregularly shaped environment spatially for use in various applications. This concept can be applied to biological organisms' spatial knowledge formation and is particularly relevant to animals' geographic knowledge representation. By examining the processes underlying spatial learning in animals such as honeybees and desert ants, it becomes apparent that their navigation methods are not necessarily driven by cognitive representations of geography. Drawing from reinforcement learning's findings, we present a new model based on two key insights: (1) spatial learning is the result of an irregular terrain's topological transformation and (2) memory's association with specific locations plays a crucial role in this process. We demonstrate that this model is equally applicable to animals' spatial learning mechanisms and the formation of geographic knowledge. Furthermore, this model offers novel insights into understanding and predicting animals' spatial behavior. This work serves as a lesson, illustrating that biological representation of geography can be intrinsically associated with local memory and topological transformation, and is therefore entirely unrelated to cognitive maps. We propose that our finding may also influence the development of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly those utilizing geographic information systems (GIS), and provide a framework for integrating our approach into a GIS system. This work is a preliminary investigation, and we plan to further examine the geographic information processing in animals, as well as the potential applications and implications of our findings. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to a deeper understanding of biological representation of geography and inspire new approaches in geographic information systems, reinforcement learning, and cognitive systems. We also expect that our findings will facilitate the development of innovative methods for integrating topological transformation and local memory into reinforcement learning systems, and have demonstrated the efficacy of this approach using a simple artificial life (A-Life) simulator. Ultimately, we intend to investigate how this concept can be applied to understand and predict the behavior of biological and artificial agents navigating complex geographic environments. We provide a comprehensive outline of our planned research in the appendix. We also offer access to the source code of our A-Life simulator on GitHub, as well as the full dataset used for our empirical analysis on Dropbox. Additionally, we have shared the geometric measurements of the artificial terrain, used in our empirical analysis, on a public knowledge base. We anticipate that these resources will facilitate the replication of our work and enable other researchers to build upon our findings. This research develops a theoretical and visual framework for understanding how the spectrograms of narrowband signals change as their frequency and phase characteristics vary. A method is then presented for using this framework to identify patterns in datasets of spectrogram level contours, which consist of sets of time-dependent frequency power spectrum maximums, by analyzing multiple signals together. The proposed framework enables the visualization of how these frequency bands evolve over time in a geographically relevant way. Additionally, some approaches for using this framework to make predictions about unknown spectrograms based on available data are presented. We have developed a multi-layered network of adaptive spiking neurons and analyzed its behavior under two different dynamic conditions - a homogeneous phase where all neurons behave similarly and an heterogeneous phase where distinct groups of neurons exhibit unique behaviors. Our primary goal was to identify clusters of neurons with similar firing patterns in the heterogeneous phase. This goal presented a challenge because even small changes in the underlying network parameters could lead to significant and unpredictable alterations in the phase dynamics, resulting in diverse firing pattern groups. Furthermore, extracting these patterns was found to be highly sensitive to noise and changes in the network parameters. To overcome these obstacles, we designed an robust algorithm that utilizes a sparse non-negative matrix decomposition (NMD) to extract and identify the diverse firing pattern groups. Our algorithm was successful in multiple trials despite being subjected to various types of noise and significant alterations in the network parameters. We found that the homogeneous and heterogeneous phases in the spiking neural networks have distinct characteristics in their firing pattern arrangements, which can provide valuable insights into understanding how these patterns contribute to synchronization and other dynamic behaviors in neural networks. Our study lays the foundation for further investigation into the relationship between phase dynamics and the structure of neural networks. Additionally, our robust algorithm can be utilized to extract coherent patterns from complex time-series data in various fields such as neuroscience, communication systems, and weather forecasting. Our findings also highlight the potential of sparse non-negative NMD in neuroscience applications, particularly in understanding how neuronal populations with distinct firing patterns contribute to overall brain function and behavior. Our study further demonstrates that robust and reliable pattern extraction is feasible even in highly unpredictable phase dynamics, which has significant implications for neural decoding and understanding how neural circuits maintain stability and functionality. Our findings also bring to light the distinct cluster arrangements in the phase transitions and suggest that sparse non-negative NMD can be utilized to derive insights into neural circuit design and modulation. The process of conducting N-body simulations, particularly those involving many celestial bodies, can be aided by utilizing random forces as a tool for detangling complex systems.  Despite their proven effectiveness, the use of random forces in low-level N-body codes may present issues due to these codes' limited memory capabilities and strict structure. This work involves re-implementing the N-body simulation code REBOUND x1e5 using the Valgrind memory error detector to specifically address how random forces are executed.  Our aim is to demonstrate the feasibility of integrating random forces into existing N-body codes.  Results from REBOUND show that random forces can be executed without inducing memory errors, even with the constraints of low memory availability, thus validating their use in future N-body simulations. 

Keywords: N-body simulations, random forces, REBOUND, Valgrind, memory error detection, celestial mechanics, astrodynamics. 

For the benefit of readers from the N-body simulation community, the code used in this study has been made publicly accessible at the following link: https://github.com/GGrillot/REBOUND_random_forces. 

This research was carried out under the supervision of Sylvain Cavero-Palmer in close collaboration with with Sebastien Colombi and the guidance of Martin Penni. 

I specifically contributed to this project by explaining the principles of N-body simulations, integrating random forces into the REBOUND code, detecting potential memory errors, and documenting the execution process. 

This work has been completed as a final project for the 'Astrodynamics' master's course at the University of Lyon under the supervision of Dr. Michael Solt and Dr. Christophe Charbonnel. 

This research has significant implications for the N-body simulation community due to its broad range of applications including modeling star clusters and other complex celestial systems. 

Upon reviewing the relevant literature, I found that the execution of random forces in N-body simulations has not been extensively explored despite their proven effectiveness, particularly in low-level codes and scenarios with many celestial bodies. 

As a result, the integration of random forces into existing N-body codes such as REBOUND presents novel challenges due to memory constraints and the strict structure of these codes. 

To address this, we have re-implemented the REBOUND code using the Valgrind memory error detector to specifically execute random forces. 

Our results show that random forces can be executed without inducing memory errors, thus validating their use in future N-body simulations, particularly those involving many celestial bodies.

A fundamental aspect of the connection between lattice and electronic properties in materials is the electron-phonon interaction. This interaction involves the exchange of momentum between electrons and ions, influenced significantly by the inertia of both entities. In this study, we explore how both electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions are intensified by the inertia of both electrons and holes, due to their equal mass. We demonstrate the significance of this effect in systems with extremely weak binding between spins and lattice vibrations, especially when temperature or energy levels are high. In such situations, our findings reveal the emergence of non-equilibrium dynamics that diverge from the conventional description of static electron-phonon interactions. We illustrate the impact of this effect in two specific materials: the superconductor PbWTe and the topological insulator with large band gap EuIn2Te4. In both cases, the interaction induces counter-intuitive dynamics, including the transfer of energy from holes to lattice vibrations and the separation of spin and charge currents. Furthermore, we show that these dynamics could be manipulated to generate high-intensity, coherent spin waves at room temperature and enable novel spin-transfer torque effects. Additionally, we propose that these dynamics could be utilized to develop new thermoelectrics capable of converting excess heat into high-voltage electric currents. Finally, we suggest that our approach could be extended to investigate collective transport within photonic systems with intrinsic nonlinear interactions. In this context, we predict the observation of nonlinear photon-radiation and propose a setup to demonstrate this phenomenon experimentally. Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering inertial effects in electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, revealing unique dynamic phenomena that could be harnessed to control electronic and spin transport and generate unique outcomes. These findings could lead to novel applications in modern nanodevices that merge magnon, photon, and charge electronics. In particular, we envision the development of innovative products like photonic and thermoelectric devices, where the inherent inertia of particles triggers extraordinary phenomena. These devices could be utilized to generate high-intensity, coherent spin waves and direct electric currents from excessive heat. In the future, we anticipate that our understanding of inertial electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions will open new avenues for innovative technology development. These developments could be based on static electron-phonon interactions, as well as novel nonlinear effects resulting from momentum transfer between electrons and ions. Lastly, we suggest that our findings may contribute to breakthroughs in photonic and thermoelectric research, as well as novel applications

Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models often underperform for new ads that have never been seen during training, causing a notable forecast error gap. To bridge this gap, we present a simple and effective framework that incorporates the actual visual content of new ads. This is achieved by leveraging a pre-trained computer vision model to extract key characteristics from each new ad and feeding these characteristics into a pre-trained CTR model. By incorporating the visual characteristics, the CTR model's forecasting capabilities are enhanced for new ads, reducing the error gap by at least 1.5% and up to 4.5% in terms of click quantity. Moreover, our approach outperforms existing ad visual feature extraction methods, yielding improved results. Crucially, the effectiveness of our framework is not dependent on the specific CTR model used, as long as it is a black-box model that takes textual input. Additionally, our framework's benefits can also extend to other scenarios, such as forecasting other ad response metrics. The code for our framework is openly accessible on GitHub. Experimental evaluations were carried out using the public dataset Adelta for evaluation purposes. Promising future research directions are also identified. The impact of our framework was validated by means of statistical significance testing. The number of additional clicks per million ads corresponds to approximately 1.28 extra clicks per day for an e-commerce platform with 1 million daily ads. The proposed framework's integration into a production ad auction system would result in improved user experience and increased revenue for the ad display platform. The proposed framework is a practical solution that is ready for implementation in real-world ad auction systems as well as other settings involving the forecasting of ad responses based on visual content. A novel approach utilizing physics-based statistical methods is formulated to integrate multi-source satellite data streams and incorporate prior knowledge from geostationary satellites. Recent advancements in technology have made it possible for a variety of service providers to offer location tracking services with unparalleled accuracy. However, this has significant implications for individual privacy as well. Existing location tracking algorithms that utilize unconditional Gaussian priors may still compromise user confidentiality. In an attempt to address this concern, this study investigates the efficacy of replacing unconditional priors with conditional priors that take into account real-world traffic patterns. Specifically, this research examines the performance of two conditional priors derived from the INLA spatial model. The results indicate that incorporating the INLA priors can result in reduced kernel density estimates that minimize the disclosure of sensitive location information. Moreover, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of the priors in a real-world location tracking scenario by leveraging the open street map data. Finally, this study evaluates the degree to which the INLA priors limit the tracing of individuals' location history. The findings suggest that the priors can substantially limit third-party surveillance of an individual's location history. In particular, this study shows that the priors can reduce third-party surveillance by at least 85%. The priors can potentially be applied in various location-based services such as road pricing, fleet management, and delivery services to enhance user privacy while maintaining service functionality. Furthermore, the priors have significant practical implications for individual privacy as well as broader social privacy. In particular, the priors can prevent unauthorized access to sensitive location information, thus protecting individuals' privacy and maintaining social anonymity. The code and data used in this study have been publicly contributed to facilitate future research on location tracking privacy. In particular, this study has made available a Python package that integrates the INLA priors with the Skippy location tracking library. Furthermore, this study has shared a dataset containing synthetic location information and traffic pattern data. The dataset can be accessed through the GitHub repository: https://github.com/tajerde/LocationTrackingPrivacy. The results can be replicated using the following command: python replicate_results.py. The resulting output will include the reduced kernel density estimates and the results can be visualized as follows: python visualize_results.py. The findings indicate that the INLA priors can significantly reduce kernel density estimates and limit third-party surveillance of an individual's location information. Brain connectivity patterns, derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), serve as a common tool for studying brain interactions and function. To investigate whether connecting individual brain sites statistically can provide accurate predictions, researchers examined the link between rs-fMRI and cognitive performance in subsets of sites within a small brain region. By simulating various sizes of connections and types of relationships between these subsets, they discovered through data analysis that the precision of resulting models was greatest when using subsets of rs-fMRI data that accurately represent the underlying brain structure. Notably, despite restricting the data to a single brain hemisphere, they were able to obtain comparable prediction results to those found in previous studies that used comprehensive rs-fMRI data. Ultimately, the findings highlight the importance of ensuring statistical methods used to study brain connections do not introduce bias when examining individual brain sites in isolation. Additionally, the results raise implications for future studies that attempt to understand and modify brain functioning based on rs-fMRI data, particularly when it comes to identifying and targeting individual brain circuits. The approaches employed in this research can be applied to various fields beyond computational neuroscience, including statistics and machine learning, to identify potential biases in target selection. Moreover, the study paves the way for further investigations into the efficacy of systematic approaches in understanding and modifying brain functioning. The code used for generating simulated rs-fMRI data, along with analysis and modeling procedures, is available at https://github.com/corntoken/rsfMRI_Subsets. We found that the transition to a low-pressure metallic state is hindered by an increased phonon mode influence and a greater pressure gap, and that this gap exhibits a greater sensitivity to pressure variations when the density of states is low. We also observed that the critical temperature of the low-pressure metallic state is highly dependent on the density of states and follows a linear relationship with the pressure gap size, and that isotopic influences are amplified in systems that exhibit a high van Hove density of states. These findings suggest that achieving superconductivity in H$_3$S will require bridging a significant gap in the material's density of states, and that isotopic influences could be crucial in realizing this superconducting state. However, we note that our analysis is limited to a tight-binding model and does not account for disorder or other real-world complications that might affect the material's behavior. Furthermore, we used a simplified model of the phonon mode's influence on the material's density of states, and our results might be modified if a more sophisticated model of the phonon structure is utilized. Nonetheless, our analysis provides a fundamental understanding of the material's properties and highlights the significance of the van Hove singularity in governing the transitions and interactions within the H$_3$S system. Additionally, we observed that our results are also applicable to other hydride superconductors such as clathrate compounds like lonsdaleite carbon (C$_2$H) and that the van Hove singularity plays a critical role in their superconducting properties. We noted an interesting correlation between our analysis of the H$_3$S system and the experimental results of the clathrate compound, and our results may have similar implications for understanding the behavior of this other superconducting material. Learning-based visual relocalization techniques have gained significance in recent years; however, these methods often depend on intense computational resources and lack comprehensive geometric information, which can impact their robustness and efficiency. This paper introduces a novel method that combines surveyor map technology with learning-based features to enhance relocalization within unknown environments. Our approach features a unique fusion of geometric and appearance information to provide robust feature descriptors. Real-world data was used to test and evaluate our system, which demonstrated its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of robustness and efficiency without any additional computational burden. Federated learning has a unique advantage in maintaining data privacy by preventing the transmission of data. Nonetheless, when combined with semi-supervised learning, it encounters a dual challenge of managing label ambiguity and requiring fewer labels to protect private data. We address these challenges by introducing a novel framework called CAR-FSL that uses unsupervised label resolution and adaptive label demand techniques. Specifically, we leverage a pseudo-labeling technique to assign a single, clear label to data sets sharing similar characteristics in the global model. Moreover, we adjust the labeling requirement based on the confidence of local models, thereby ensuring a labelling budget that optimally balances data labeling and model performance. Our experiments on standard datasets and a clinical dataset from the Mayo Clinic show improvements over the current best approaches in terms of accuracy, adaptation, and data utilization. particular, we achieve superior performance with limited labels compared to conventional FL-SSL methods. Our car-FSL approach outperforms SSL methods in a label-rich setting and delivers comparable results to state-of-the-art FL-SSL methods in a label-poor setting. A comprehensive evaluation of modeling decisions, data efficiency, and user participation reveals our car-FSL approach to offer significant improvements in these areas. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of CAR-FSL's adaptive label assignment strategy and highlight the importance of data types in the informed design of federated semi-supervised learning algorithms. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/learn2bepecific/car-fsl. We believe our contributions will facilitate the development of innovative adaptations of FL-SSL that prioritize data privacy and performance. Specifically, we estimate that our car-FSL approach leads to a data reduction of 40\% compared to the best available FL-SSL methods without compromising on performance. Additionally, we achieve this improvement while ensuring that the label quality remains 95\% accurate due to our unsupervised label resolution technique. A thorough analysis of our results and the complex interplay between label ambiguity and data privacy in FL-SSL informs our conclusions. We hope our research will facilitate the creation of performance and privacy-aware adaptations of FL-SSL techniques. The concept of team synchrony is defined as a phenomenon where different team members exhibit coherent and distinct rhythmic patterns within the same time frame. In this research, we explore how various factors influence team synchrony in a scenario involving cat-and-mouse foraging behavior, using an agent-based model that incorporates individual characteristics and social interactions. Our findings demonstrate that team synchrony emerges and is maintained through a process of selection, and reveal three underlying mechanisms through which team members become synchronized: timely alignment, shared activity, and mutual stabilization of rhythms. Additionally, our results show that team synchrony is enhanced when team members have similar parameters and engage in social interactions, but can also thrive in diverse teams that interact with each other. However, when teams compete rather than cooperate, the emergence of synchronized rhythms is reduced, and discrepancies within a team's parameters negatively impact its ability to maintain synchronized rhythms. Overall, our study highlights the significance of social interactions in stabilizing and refining rhythmic patterns, and demonstrates that diverse teams can still exhibit stable and coherent patterns of behavior. These findings have implications for understanding the role of social interactions in the development and maintenance of coordinated behaviors in living systems. Although the specific example used in this research is based on animal behavior, the underlying mechanisms of team synchrony are likely to be relevant to a broader range of domains, including human teams and social groups. Our analysis also offers insights into designing and improving coordinated systems, such as software or human teams, by highlighting the importance of both individual diversity and social interactions in maintaining stable and coherent patterns of activity. At a deeper level, this research sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of coordination and the role of social interactions in shaping the behavior and structure of social groups, and explores the broader implications of these ideas for understanding and interacting with the world around us. To overcome these limitations, a new method called PatchNet is proposed, which calculates pixel positions directly from detected patches without requiring interpolation. This approach is simple, fast, and accurate, particularly for high-resolution videos, where it outperforms the area-based method in terms of speed and precision. Furthermore, PatchNet is adaptable to a range of video processing tasks, including super-resolution, motion analysis, and object detection, where the alignment of templates is essential. To illustrate the efficacy of this approach, PatchNet is applied to various video processing tasks within a Deep Neural Network (DNN) framework, where it yields satisfactory results and demonstrates faster processing times compared to the area-based method. The source code for PatchNet is publicly available, enabling researchers to integrate this approach into their research and development efforts. Experimental evaluations confirm that PatchNet is a more efficient and accurate solution for video processing tasks, specifically when dealing with high-resolution inputs, where it outperforms the area-based method in terms of speed and precision. Preoperative planning for gastric surgery often relies on accurate CT scans, yet these images may be difficult to interpret due to smoke and water droplets interfering with the surgeon's visibility during the procedure.  To resolve this, we investigated whether enhancing the quality of laparoscopic images using preoperative data could benefit smoke identification.  To this end, we used a deep neural network to automatically remove smoke and water droplets from images taken during the procedure, then evaluated whether this process improved smoke detection.  Specifically, we compared the performance of a model trained on smoke-free images with Laplacian Pyramidal Decomposition and a model trained on augmented images corrected for smoke and water using the preoperative data, on a dataset of 36 laparoscopic videos containing smoke and water droplets.  The subsequent experiments involved simulating smoke and water droplets on gastric surgery videos, followed by a comparison of the results with those obtained through human observation, revealing that the improved quality of the images benefited smoke detection although the methods differed in their approach to image enhancement.  Consequently, we suggest that future studies on smoke detection should consider image enhancement as an alternative strategy to simply filtering the images. Researchers introduced a novel conceptual framework for analyzing the behavioral patterns of optimization algorithms averaging certain problems together. This framework, called average-case complexity theory, allows researchers to study real-world optimization challenges by combining multiple problems with varying levels of difficulty. In this theoretical context, a crucial question arises about the nature of optimization problems themselves, specifically: which problems are efficiently solvable and which are inherently difficult? We investigate this question by developing more refined metrics that measure optimization problems' relative ease or difficulty relative to others, and we explore how these metrics correlate with established problem strength metrics. Additionally, we examine how these metrics apply to problems with convex constraints and develop new techniques to study their average-case complexity. This leads to a surprising discovery: a problem's relative ease or difficulty is determined solely by the distribution of its optimal solutions, specifically their tails. We demonstrate that our findings yield valuable insights into the average-case complexity of various critical applications, such as non-convex and stochastic optimization, yielding more precise and accurate understanding of their behavioral patterns. This new perspective on optimization problems enables researchers to gain more insight into their average-case complexity, and it has far-reaching implications for how researchers study and approach optimization challenges. We also propose several future research directions that we believe are worthy of exploration. At present, there are only a few concrete examples of problems with varying levels of relative ease or difficulty. These examples set the stage for future research into how to categorize optimization problems by their average-case complexity. This, in turn, can lead to more efficient and effective solutions to optimization problems. Research on the Cotton tensor has increased significantly recently, particularly in its relation to conformal gravity theory where it acts as a Bianchi identity-derived curvature scalar. Due to this rising interest, it is essential to provide a clear, concise overview of the Cotton tensor's utility in describing gravity theory. This summary will discuss the Cotton tensor's uses in conformal gravity theory and their broader implications for general relativity and other modified gravity theories. We will also examine how it can be utilized as an alternative approach to describe these theories. Furthermore, recent findings in gauge non-invariant formulations of gravity and their relationship to Weyl postulate, particularly in 3D and 4D spacetimes with and without a Chern-Simons term, will be highlighted. Finally, recent research on coupled Poincaré and spin-2 gravities in both flat and anti-de Sitter environments will also be reviewed. These coupled theories involve coupling Maxwell fields to gravity, which leads to key constraints on 4D conformal theories such as coupling constants and Poincaré constants being linked. This overview will serve as a primer for researchers new to the subject while also highlighting exciting areas for further research within the field of the Cotton tensor. In particular, we will explore how it can contribute to developing a more comprehensive and coherent description of gravity theory. The Cotton tensor might play a crucial role in this endeavor due to its unique properties and broad applicability to various theories. It is specifically well-suited for describing the interaction between spin-2 and vector fields, which is a key feature of conformal gravity theory. This summary will also examine recent research on generalized Cotton tensors and their potential for further extension and generalization in novel 4D conformal curvatures theories. These theories were recently introduced and demonstrated to have a curved spacetime equivalent derived from the Cotton tensor's curvature scalar properties. The relationship between curvature and curvature-squared theories and their equivalence to Einstein and conformally Einstein theories in four dimensions will also be discussed. The summary will conclude with an overview of key challenges and unsolved problems in the field. It will also propose future research directions such as further studying coupled Poincaré and spin-2 theories in anti-de Sitter spacetimes and exploring research opportunities in generalized Cotton tensors and 4D conformal curvature theories. The latter may provide valuable insights into the behavior of compact gravitational objects such as black holes and black holes with scalar hair due to their fundamental link to curvature and curvature-squared in these types of spacetimes. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is finite by utilizing the representation theory of $\mathrm{GL}(2)$, drawing specifically from the asymptotic count of its degree two irreducible automorphic representations with a sufficiently large spectral parameter. This approach builds upon the work of Sato and the findings of Iwaniec, which focused on the logarithm of the determinant of the Laplacian and the representation theory of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. Furthermore, our method allows for the derivation of an asymptotic formula for the fourth moment of Hecke cusp forms modified by a power function. This outcome is a by-product of our investigation into the distribution of eigenvalues of the Laplacian, combining principles from the geometry of modular forms and the representation theory of $\mathrm{GL}(2)$. Additionally, we make notable observations regarding the counts of irreducible automorphic representations according to their properties and the behavior of certain Dirichlet L-functions at critical values. These have significant implications for the fourth moment of all holomorphic cusp forms and deduce a variant of the Sato-type conjecture for Hecke cusp forms, yielding a sharp bound on the fourth moment as claimed in the title. Lastly, our work on the distribution of eigenvalues of the Laplacian sheds new light on the asymptotic distribution of the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on the upper half-plane with its action modified by a power function. This is a consequence of our findings and the established connections between modular forms and the representation theory of $\mathrm{GL}(2)}$.

Recent years have seen significant growth in AI technology, leading to its adoption in high-stakes systems, yet this acceleration has been accompanied by an alarming increase in AI system failures. This proliferation of errors, ranging from minor discrepancies to life-threatening mistakes, poses a significant risk of severe harm. Understanding that documenting transportation accidents (the Air Safety Incident System) and medical errors (the National Practitioner Data Bank) have helped to learn from past mistakes and prevent future occurrences, a team has created the AI Incident Repository (AIIR) to record common pitfalls and failures in AI systems. By collecting real-world case studies of AI system failures, AIIR aims to provide crucial knowledge for avoiding similar mistakes in the future. This approach will offer crucial input to discussions on standardized failure reporting and the incorporation of failure experiences into the AI community's collective knowledge, enabling more efficient learning from past errors and preventing the recurrence of mistakes. The AIIR, now accessible on the web at aiincidents.org, welcomes contributions of real-world failure stories and incidents, and will continuously evolve based on community input and feedback. Early efforts have already yielded a diverse collection of 300+ failure stories spanning 10 domains, and preliminary analyses have identified recurring failure patterns and themes across various domains. As the AIIR grows, it will provide a comprehensive failure experience database and facilitate research on how failures across different domains can inform and learn from each other. The AIIR's failure collection and analytics capabilities will be made available under a permissive license to foster a shared understanding of failures throughout the AI community. The team is now exploring how AIIR failures, and particularly failure-causing technologies and scenarios, can be leveraged to inform the development of more reliable AI systems, and evaluating the accuracy of failure taxonomies and the replication rates of failed systems, among other key research questions. With a wide range of potential research directions, AIIR is positioned to become a vital knowledge resource for advancing the safety and reliability of AI systems. The team is now seeking contributions, participation, and support to further develop and utilize the AIIR. The emergence of single-molecule, long-read sequencing technologies has greatly enhanced the accuracy of genome assembly, particularly for repeat-rich and large genomes. Nevertheless, constructing a complete and closed genome using these sequences remains computationally and computationally intensive. One crucial step in the sequencing process, baits production, can be accelerated through the utilization of graphics processing units (GPUs). Nevertheless, the increasing availability of distributed-memory systems via Clustered GPU configurations necessitates the development of scalable software for baits production. This paper introduces a new, parallel approach for producing baits, in which each node generates random contigs independently, and the overall process is divided into sequential stages to ensure easy management and adaptation to differing memory capacities across nodes. Our method shows promising potential for assembling large and complex genomes with unparalleled accuracy. The developed software can efficiently produce the desired baits on standard hardware at an unprecedentedly rapid pace, specifically by methodologies that make use of clustered GPU configurations. A thorough evaluation of our method was carried out using a comprehensive combination of real-world and artificially created datasets. The results demonstrate a linear correlation between the number of available nodes and memory and the overall speedup in baits production. This promising finding suggests the method could reach a peak speed-up of up to $24.6\times$ with $62$ nodes. Furthermore, a substantial reduction in runtime was achieved via the use of parallelism, with a particular decline observed when working with large, specific-type genomes. The developed software is now freely accessible under the BSD-2 license at a specified website. Additionally, the relevant code has been thoroughly documented, detailing its functionality at length, as well as the employed data and configuration settings, which have been made available for reproduction of the presented results. The software can be employed for a broad range of sequencing-related applications, such as genome assembly, the construction of supracohorts, and more, using a comprehensive list of specified parameters. A flexible interface allows for the easy adaptation of the software to differing memory capacities across nodes at multiple stages. Furthermore, a novel "split-and-generate" approach was employed, in which sequential stages manage independent node processes to prevent memory overload, as well as the introduction of a novel, efficient data structure, specifically designed for the management of repeated sequences in baits production. This novel approach not only leads to a speed-up but also decreases memory usage by a significant amount, especially when working with large sequences. Moreover, a related problem was identified and a novel, efficient algorithm was developed to solve it, specifically by merging sequences.

This study focuses on the dynamics of an equation that was derived from models used to analyze population growth in biology. By introducing a delay into the logistic equation, we examined its impact on modeling periodic phenomena in biology. This analysis revealed that the combined effects of population growth rate and delay result in fundamentally different dynamics than traditional logistic models. Our investigation included linearization and stability analysis of both the equation and its corresponding discrete model. These findings showed that the continuous model exhibits unique behaviors, such as the coexistence of two unstable equilibrium points in a periodic solution. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the continuous model exhibits novel global patterns, such as periodic solutions that are biologically relevant, while the discrete model only exhibits periodic, oscillating solutions. Our analysis also revealed that these global patterns are trapped in an attracting set, preventing it from converging to a stable equilibrium. Our theoretical results were validated through numerical simulations and visualizations. Our approaches have been successfully demonstrated on simulated point data sets and also on species data from the Kruger National Park. A century after their discovery, superconducting hybrid devices continue to be a cornerstone of basic scientific research and cutting-edge technological development. However, traditional devices often struggle with two significant drawbacks: they're prone to thermal fluctuations that hinder their performance, and the varying properties of individual devices make them difficult to study. To overcome these limitations, our work focuses on an all-manganite nanowire device that showcases an ideal hybrid geometry, with the potential to revolutionize the field of superconducting device research. By utilizing this component, we've achieved the longest hybrid device length and the longest hybrid device frequency response, along with an exceptionally high ratio of length to resistance. Our findings serve as a benchmark for hybrid devices, and the techniques used to fabricate them could lead to breakthroughs in hybrid electronic and photonic devices, including those that utilize all-manganite materials. Through our research, we've discovered an unexpected length scale that affects device performance, and our data indicate the presence of multiple length-dependent hybrid modes. Additionally, our study has revealed an ideal hybrid device characteristic: the ratio of length to resistance is independent of device width and is influenced solely by device length. We introduce an original approach to determining isochronous stable-time-of-flight mass spectra using the $B\rho$-defined ion optical system at the mass spectrometry beam line in RIKEN Nishina Center. This method acknowledges the inherent limitations imposed by the systemic errors rooted in the ion optics, where the actual trajectories deviate from the ideal path. Rather than striving for error-free performance, our method focuses on minimizing the impact of these systematic flaws. As a result, even with existing technical constraints, high-precision mass measurements of short-lived nuclei can be achieved. This technique was further illustrated using simulated calculations based on the actual experimental settings used at the RIKEN Nishina Center. Our results demonstrate the potential for reducing systematic uncertainties related to the time-of-flight by up to four orders of magnitude, which could significantly contribute to future mass evaluations. This new approach is expected to significantly enhance our understanding of precise mass measurements. Additionally, this method is versatile and can be easily adapted to various $B\rho$-defined ion optical systems, particularly those with a magnetic or electrostatic structure. This breakthrough may open new avenues for investigating physics related to exotic nuclei and dark matter using high-precision mass measurements that were previously considered inaccessible. This novel approach could significantly expand our knowledge in both theoretical and experimental physics, which is particularly relevant to the research priorities at the RIKEN Nishina Center and similar research facilities worldwide. Our findings indicate that this method can significantly contribute to precision mass measurements, which might be particularly useful for investigations at the RIKEN Nishina Center. Our study strongly suggests that further studies using the RIKEN Nishina Center's facilities, particularly for the $^{42}$K-$^{42}$K isochronous mass spectrometry, be carried out to demonstrate the full potential of this approach. This method has far-reaching implications and we propose to carry out the remaining experiments needed to demonstrate its full capabilities. Our proposed experimental strategy includes two specific research directions, namely the high-precision mass measurements of $^{26}$O and $^{34}$P, which could significantly contribute to our understanding of the atomic mass evaluation table. Our study indicates that even with existing technical constraints, high-precision mass measurements of short-lived nuclei can be achieved using the $B\rho$-defined isochronous stable-time-of-flight method.
