The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally and reached China's shores in January 2020, where the spread was initially exacerbated by rumors. The impact of these rumors was particularly concerning given the public's fear of the disease. The dissemination of rumors was concerning as it could jeopardize the public's health by encouraging non-compliant behavior and heightening public anxiety. This study aims to examine the spread of rumors in China during the outbreak, specifically focusing on the initial spread, the influence of news sources, and the predictive factors of rumor dissemination. We also assess the effect of rumors on people's behavior, revealing a noticeable impact on anxiety levels among those who engage with rumors. Just like regular news, rumors spread faster on social media and are predicted to disseminate further when they receive early support from influential users. However, our findings also show that rumors are more likely to spread faster and further when they originate from unknown sources, particularly during times of public crisis. The influence of news sources on the spread of rumors varies, with government and local news sources generally having a negative impact, whereas international news sources may have a positive effect, potentially due to their objective nature. The predictive factors of rumor dissemination include viral characteristics, social network properties, and temporal factors, with rumors that are about everyday life and have clear themes tend to disseminate further, as opposed to those with ambiguous themes. Finally, our research reveals that rumors do have an impact on people's behavior, particularly when it comes to anxiety levels, where there are noticeable differences between those who engage with and those who do not engage with rumors. In terms of magnitude, the impact of rumors is comparable to that of regular news, while there are also significant individual differences in how people respond to rumors. Our research used machine learning algorithms to model and predict the dissemination of rumors, revealing a substantial 70% accuracy in predicting the spread of rumors. Based on these findings, we propose several practical strategies to control the spread of rumors, while also emphasizing the need for further long-term research on this topic. Additionally, our data and related materials are available for download. We expect our research to contribute to the understanding of online rumor dissemination and its impact, while also generating valuable insights for future studies. Moreover, our research can be applied to develop algorithms that accurately predict the dissemination of rumors, thereby enabling more effective decision-making in areas of public interest. Finally, our research has implications for communicating effective information during public crises, while also providing valuable knowledge that can be utilized for combating misinformation campaigns. Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing have primarily been fueled by massive advancements in natural language models. Despite the impressive results, it has become increasingly difficult and costly to make further improvements. Our research focuses on exploring alternative approaches that are less built on pre-trained models, yet still leverage their learned knowledge. Specifically, we investigate the reduction of deep neural models using formal concept analysis and multiple kernel learning techniques. Our key contributions are (a) developing a novel reduction method for deep neural networks, (b) introducing a new attention mechanism for multi-task learning, and (c) testing this approach on various language understanding datasets, including SST, TASS, TASC, and CoQA. Experimental results indicate that our reduced models, re-trained from weight matrices, can outperform the original models, especially on tasks like text classification and natural language inference. Our reduced models, featuring a smaller architecture and fewer parameters, also demonstrate similar or better performance on question answering and sentiment analysis. Our proposed reduction methods are now being made publicly available for the benefit of the natural language processing community. It is worth noting that while our reduced models may not use pre-trained knowledge, it is possible to adapt the reduction methods to incorporate external knowledge for even better results. Our work has promising implications for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of deep neural models, especially multi-head attention-based models, and we believe this research may lead to new developments in model reduction and knowledge adaptation. Our code is available at https://github.com/jbarnesspain/natural-language-reduction if you would like to replicate the results or try the methods ourselves. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, has been introduced to validate and improve protein structures by accurately estimating the chemical shifts of amide protons. This prediction method leverages quantum mechanics to model the effects of resonance Raman dispersion and vibrational coupling on chemical shifts, explaining about 90% of differences between predicted and actual values. ProCS has been used to verify the quality of protein structures, revealing a correlation between residual error and protein complexity, with errors increasing for more complex systems. Furthermore, ProCS has been applied to improve protein structures by minimizing total error, both absolute and relative, leading to improvements of up to 30% in overall residue accuracy in test cases. To better understand the impact of loss functions, we conducted an extensive meta-analysis involving 1,304 experiments from the top cited machine learning conferences over the last ten years. Our analysis reveals that using a dynamic loss function in conjunction with data augmentation yields superior classification results in all scenarios we examined, including both supervised and semi-supervised learning procedures. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that incorporating loss function variation enhances the stability and reliability of models, particularly in the training and validation phases of the model's lifetime. To facilitate future advancements, we also outline potential paths for continued research and present a versatile, efficient class-balanced loss function that surpasses performance of established loss functions, including cross-entropy, in certain circumstances. Our code is freely accessible on the following platform: https://github.com/jbmanwaring/loss_experiments. Keywords: Deep Learning, Loss Functions, Neural Networks, Classification, Meta-Analysis.

To properly manage electronic states, it is essential to employ a relativistic band-structure calculation for 2D layered semiconducting materials, as their electronic states near the Fermi level are inherently anisotropic and exhibit high momenta. Despite being necessary, relativistic band structure calculations are often avoided due to increased computational complexity. In this study, we demonstrate the feasibility of a more advanced ab initio approach for studying complex electronic phenomena in 2D semiconducting materials. As a test case, we investigate the exciton liquefaction of these materials using TiSe2 as an example. Furthermore, we also discuss the possibility of observing a superconducting state in 2D materials that exhibit exciton liquefaction. Our findings suggest that the primary mechanism underlying the charge density wave (CDW) in TiSe2 is meditated by electron-exciton interaction, leading to the onset of a new phase of matter known as a liquid exciton superfluid. In this state, the correlation energy associated with excitons triggers the condensation of quasiparticles into a sublattice of electron holes, thereby generating a charge density wave in TiSe2. In order to describe these phenomena, we employed a novel ab initio approach, which combines relativistic band structure calculations with more advanced ab initio methods such as many-body theory and density functional theory, while also incorporating lattice dynamics. Our test case, TiSe2, exhibits a unique property where the wave number of the charge density wave matches the peak of the electron-hole fluid's form factor, thereby confirming that the interaction between electrons and holes plays a crucial role in determining the phase of the material. Our findings also suggest that the onset of charge density wave in TiSe2 is a first-order phase transition, which is consistent with experimental observations of the material. Our study offers a new understanding of the role of electron-hole interactions in the phase transitions of 2D semiconducting materials, which is likely to be applicable to other materials such as 2H-NbSe2. Moreover, we speculate that the onset of charge density wave in these materials may also occur in other phases of the superconducting and exciton-liquid states. Police dispatchers play a vital role in community safety, facilitating effective emergency responses by accurately assessing caller reports and providing timely instructions. However, discrepancies between written reports submitted by community members and verbal communications with dispatchers can reveal valuable insights into user-interaction experiences. Current natural language processing (NLP) techniques primarily focus on the written reports, neglecting the concealed knowledge hidden in conversational records. To address this gap, we developed a text-oriented system for analyzing dispatcher-caller interactions using a combination of textual data and codified behavioral indicators. Through statistical analysis of a large dataset comprising 17,341 incident reports from dispatchers, our findings uncover significant patterns, including the correlation between interaction experiences and incident types, the variation in interaction experiences across different areas, and the relationship between dispatching periods and incident categories. Furthermore, our system's usability was validated through user evaluations, demonstrating its practical value in practical applications. The presented approach can be applied to other contexts of human-machine interaction to yield valuable insights into user experiences. A real-world example of this approach is provided in the form of a video available under doi: 10.17632/874927f7d7b60b7c22c1d7d1e7d1e.

This method employs visually driven clustering algorithms to group items in a manner that aligns with human assessments, using labeled data from multiple human sources. To facilitate time-effective learning, we adapted this method for both static and dynamic environments. In the field of Machine Learning, using hash tables to track objects' locations is a common practice, often requiring an inverse search to find all objects that match a specific condition after a hash table transformation has been applied. This can be achieved through a faster algorithm than brute force by utilizing a concept known as generalized convolution, allowing for looking up all objects related to a specific query in a single operation. This research presents an efficient, max-min hash-based solution for generalized convolution, capable of optimizing the processing speed of hash table-based queries.

A crucial component of our solution is a novel, fast algorithm for calculating the generalized convolution of two sets of points in $d$-dimensional space. This algorithm leverages the use of separators, specifically hyperplanes, to split the space and achieve faster calculation times than previous methods. We have derived a theoretical proof that demonstrates the optimal time complexity for this calculation task, outperforming earlier approaches.

To further enhance the performance of our solution, we also developed a strategy for reducing the number of hyperplanes involved in the calculation process. This is accomplished by combining adjacent regions of the space and reducing the number of hyperplanes, resulting in improved efficiency.

Our max-min hash-based solution for generalized convolution is accompanied by a method for generating random hyperplanes with specific properties. These 'friendly' hyperplanes are used to optimize the calculation process and allow for the use of efficient sorting techniques to further improve performance.

We have thoroughly evaluated our solution by comparing its performance to other approaches, specifically general convolution methods and those using binary trees, in a range of scenarios. The results of these experiments demonstrate that our solution significantly outperforms other approaches, resulting in speedups of up to 50 times, depending on the specific conditions. Moreover, our solution exhibits consistent and predictable performance, even when dealing with diverse data sets and query types. Consequently, our solution is an ideal choice for applications that require fast general convolution calculations, such as query processing in databases and machine learning-based object detection tasks. Additionally, we have developed an open-source library that allows for the easy integration of our solution into various machine learning applications. Further details on the theoretical foundations, as well as the library, can be found at the website specified in the corresponding author section.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis has been lacking.  The authors applied the APOLLO retrieval code to the existing spectral data of GJ 229B, which suggested that the dwarf has a methane-rich atmosphere with internal heat sources generating fluxes significantly higher than model predictions for late T-dwarfs.  The code indicated that GJ 229B's internal energy production is comparable to Jupiter's, which can be attributed to accretion of solid particles from the planet's formation environment.  The researchers also explored the possibility of GJ 229B being a brown dwarf instead of a T-dwarf, which would require it to have a much stronger H-alpha emission than expected for a late T-dwarf, as well as being older and more massive than initially thought.  The underlying nature of GJ 229B's energy source, which could be an ordinary T-dwarf or an object of significantly more massive material, remains a subject of debate and further observation.  The authors suggested that future direct spectral observations of GJ 229B in the 1.1-2.2 micron range could confirm the presence of methane, carbon dioxide, or other solubles in its atmosphere, which would help to clarify the dwarf's composition.  The researchers also estimated the object to be in a highly eccentric orbit around a low-mass star, which could lead to the depletion of solid particles in the atmosphere through orbital processes.  The authors hypothesized that this could result in a more conventional sub-TeV sub-mass late T-dwarf composition if the dwarf's atmosphere were to be resupplied with solid particles.  The researchers also noted that GJ 229B's internal heat could be a result of the object's rapid contraction due to its unusually high mass, which would be a rare phenomenon in the late T-dwarf category.  The authors pointed out that further analysis of other T-dwarfs with infrared spectra could help to confirm whether GJ 229B's exceptional properties are unique or shared by other late T-dwarfs.  The researchers also applied the APOLLO code to model the properties of other known T-dwarfs, which did not reveal any internal heat sources or extraordinary atmospheric features.  The authors speculated that GJ 229B may be an object of a life stage, which could transform from an unusual 'hot' T-dwarf to a more conventional 'cold' late T-dwarf

To assess the transmission risk of infectious diseases on a urban bus, we developed and tested an analytical framework that simulates disease spread in a mixed population of susceptible and infected individuals. Our model incorporates variables such as infected person's infectious period, the urban bus's capacity, and the susceptibility population. A non-linear equation represents the change in susceptible and infected person counts over time, influenced by two distinct factors: random mixing among passengers and discrete interactions with the driver. Our analysis focuses on understanding ultimate convergence to an equilibrium state near zero, specifically the urban bus's ultimate convergence rate to the basic reproduction number (R0). A detailed examination of R0 revealed that it is a quadratic function of the urban bus's capacity, suspecting an optimal seating arrangement could minimize transmission risk. This hypothesis guided our numerical simulations, which demonstrated that seating arrangements indeed impact infection spread. Furthermore, our model was validated using two distinct urban bus scenarios, confirming our hypotheses that compartmentalized seating arrangements could minimize infection spread and that urban bus passengers may experience a decline in population due to limited seating capacity. Our study's findings are significant as they pave the way for further research into how to adapt and implement public health strategies to effectively mitigate the spread of infectious diseases on urban buses, particularly in urban areas with limited seating capacity. These strategies could involve the use of different seating arrangements, such as blocking certain seats, to minimize transmission risk. Additionally, our models can be applied to other urban environments, like taxis, to better understand and mitigate the spread of infectious diseases in urban communities. A curve in a metric space is defined as nonexpansive if the distance between two of its points is always less than or equal to the metric distance between those points. In the presence of a base metric space, a curve can be categorized as weakly cyclic or strongly cyclic based on whether it encloses a cyclic structure or forms a cyclic structure itself. With a base metric space, a curve can be further categorized as quasi-cyclic or quasi-periodic depending on whether it approximates a cyclic structure. In the absence of a base metric space, a curve can be regarded as quasi-cyclic or quasi-periodic depending on whether it approximates a cyclic structure. 
This article focuses on finding a specific type of curve decomposition given a certain set of curves containing all nonexpansive curves in a specific metric space. Additionally, this article proves that quasi-cyclic curves can be regarded as weakly cyclic curves under specific conditions. Lastly, this article presents an example of a type of metric space where quasi-cyclic curves do not necessarily form a cyclic structure. 
One significant observation from the proofs in this article is that quasi-cyclic curves may be redefined as curves that can be decomposed into a finite combination of nonexpansive curves with specific cyclic structures. This leads to an interesting consequence where quasi-cyclic curves and cyclic structures become equivalent in certain types of metric spaces. 
An alternative definition of quasi-cyclic curves has also been proposed which demands that the union of all finite combinations of nonexpansive curves with specific cyclic structures covers the entire curve, however this definition may not consistently produce the same result as the initial definition and may produce distinct results for certain curves. 
An interesting property of quasi-cyclic curves has also been identified where a quasi-cyclic curve is always composed of a mixture of quasi-periodic and weakly cyclic curves.

To efficiently learn motor tasks, robots benefit from experiencing actions that are predictable from their previous experiences.
We developed a metric to quantify this condition, called the end-effectivity degree, which measures how likely an action is to improve performance based on past experiences.
This new metric, combined with an optimized planning approach, helps robots focus on high-value experiences, leading to faster adaptation and improved performance in complex control systems.

This breakthrough enables the development of more agile and adaptable robots that can quickly learn to move efficiently in dynamic environments. encountered areas, we propose MemoNav, which selects the most relevant past
moments to aid navigation. MemoNav represents spatial relationships with a
temporal graph and employs key graph neural networks to predict the most useful
recollections for generating navigation guidance. These recollections are then
leveraged to generate instructions based on a variation of transformer models.

fields. In particular, the method proposed in this study can be adapted for

in the supplementary materials provided. We expect MemoNav and the related tools
to serve as a foundation for future research in recall-based robotic navigation.

Thermal neutron-capture reactions are crucial for understanding gamma-ray debris spectroscopy, particularly for heavy, unstable nuclei. Researchers have recently investigated this process using the LUCI array and the Beta Decay Tunnel (BDT) at the Yellow Cabin laboratory, yielding novel data on the 30S Isomer. When S30 undergoes neutron capture, it transitions into 31S, and subsequent beta plus decay leads to the 30Mg Isomer, whose de-excitation spectrum matches the Hoyle state's, thereby indicating the presence of a 8.07 MeV broad and structure-rich gamma-ray spectrum associated with this transition. Scientists have interpreted this phenomenon as the direct outcome of electronic shell effects, specifically the weakening of neutron-to-proton ratios in 31S, leading to a 30S Hoyle-state-like ground state in 30Mg, and have seen an enhancement of 75% in the isomerization probability when using a TPCC for detection, as compared to a Ge-coincidence setup. Finally, researchers have calculated the 30S Hoyle-state decay rate to be 0.106 +/- 0.013 megaseconds, a value roughly 2 times higher than the current estimate. This new finding might influence the 30S Isomer's structure and might also prompt a re-evaluation of the 30S Hoyle-state ground-state energy. Additionally, this study's results prove that the TPC is an extremely sensitive detector for pinpointing subtle nuclear changes, particularly in heavy, unstable nuclei. Consequently, future researchers could utilize this arrangement to detect minor alterations in neutron-capture reactions and to further fine-tune debris spectroscopy. Lastly, scientists have suggested the utilization of the LUCI-TPC arrangement at various accelerator facilities, including the proposed Facility for Antiproton Utilization, in order to further study thermal neutron-capture reactions and their role in stellar nucleosynthesis. This study focuses on analyzing scientific research claims related to data presented in tables.  The goal is to determine the accuracy of these claims by identifying which claims are supported by the data presented.  Additionally, we aim to enhance research efficiency by pinpointing specific rows in the data that substantiate each claim.  This task involves evaluating the effectiveness of algorithmic methods in accomplishing these objectives across two categories: verifying general research claims and locating specific data rows.  Fifty-four research papers were analyzed by a panel of expert reviewers who drew inspiration from prior efforts to establish evaluation standards for NLP and data science.  A total of 172 truth verification and 181 evidence-finding annotations were collected, accompanied by a detailed guide for incorporating these annotations into automated systems.  A panel of seven expert reviewers evaluated submissions to SemEval 2021, submitting 41 eligible submissions for review in both components of the task.  New benchmarks were established in both research areas, with submissions from 29 and 20 sources recorded in the truth verification and evidence-finding categories, respectively.  Notably, cross-disciplinary collaborations played a significant role in shaping this research initiative, with connections to the fields of natural language processing, data science, and biomedical informatics.  Future developments based on this work may yield beneficial applications in areas such as automated fact-checking and data exploration.  The data and annotation resources used in this study can be accessed via a repository at https://github.com/KnowledgeGraphs/SEM-TAB-FACTS/tree/main/data.  The code used in this research initiative is available at https://github.com/KnowledgeGraphs/SEM-TAB-FACTS. We explore the significance of complex numbers in quantum physics, examining their introduction, uses, and impact on physical principles. The study highlights the intricacy of these numbers in coupled oscillator systems, specifically for the Tamm-Shockley wave function and emitter models. Additionally, it delves into complex momentum operators in one-dimensional non-relativistic quantum mechanics. The emergence of complex frequencies in perturbation theory and complex magnetic flux in quantum electrodynamics is also examined. Finally, the essential role of complex numbers in quantum physics is emphasized. While they can be replaced with pairs of real numbers for basic problems, this is often accompanied by awkward expressions and unfamiliar solutions, highlighting the benefits of working directly with complex numbers. Ultimately, this involves reconceptualizing one's understanding of quantum physics. We suggest that this method of expression can be useful in studying quantum physics and potentially other complex physical systems. 

This work is inspired by the author's courses and lectures, particularly a graduate-level quantum mechanics course, and aims to provide an introductory overview of the topic. Due to length constraints, it presents selected findings from existing research rather than offering an extensive literature review. For a more comprehensive understanding, readers are referred to relevant research articles and textbooks. We expect that future investigations in this area will yield significant findings.

The growing demand for more efficient artificial intelligence systems has led to a surge in the development of neuromorphic hardware and its associated simulations. Standardizing the architecture and developing portable simulations can accelerate advancements, making concurrent development more feasible. Our solution is a SystemC-based framework for concurrent multi-processor architecture simulations, incorporating a hybrid transaction-level modeling of hard and soft components. It also integrates a hard processor model and a transaction-level model of a GPGPU core, capable of executing a fully parallelized simulating spiking neural network algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by utilizing a portable transaction-level model of the spiking neural network model. Our experimental results show the benefits of concurrent simulations, achieving a speedup of up to 5.57x in simulating a large neural network on a dual-core system with a dual-core GPU. Moreover, we achieved an impressive speedup of up to 10.44x in simulating a neural network on a dual-core CPU by utilizing a dual-core GPU. Our innovative approach to concurrent multi-processor simulations employs a novel transaction-level model of a hybrid CPU-GPGPU core, paving the way for more efficient neuromorphic hardware simulations in the future. As a result, this work contributes to the advancement of portable and reusable simulations, which is a crucial milestone in developing practical artificial neural systems. Experimental data, including the full simulation framework source code, is publicly accessible on GitHub. This contribution enables the computational neuroscience and hardware neuroscience communities to develop simulations more rapidly. Specifically, we demonstrated an order-of-magnitude improvement in simulating bio-inspired neural networks on software, which is a notable achievement in the field. Our work also accelerates the development of new neuromorphic hardware and emerging computing architectures by making it easier to simulate and test multiple designs concurrently. To further facilitate research, we also made available a set of useful transaction-level models of various hardware components and neural networks, which can be freely accessed and used. This collaborative effort is essential for advancing our knowledge in hardware and neuroscience, as well as emerging computing and computational neuroscience. Our test suite and simulation framework will continue to be maintained and updated on GitHub to support concurrent multi-processor architecture simulations and facilitate cutting-edge research across related domains. This collective effort is essential for accelerating the practical implementation of artificial neural systems. Our related projects listed below serve a similar purpose, including making portable and reusable simulations accessible. Specifically, we explored the potential of emulating the Google Brain deep neural network on traditional CPU architectures and demonstrated the feasibility of concurrent multi-processor simulations

Machine learning algorithms are increasingly used in safety-critical systems yet a significant limitation exists in that they typically generate certain decisions with complete confidence, even though this is not realistically the case in many situations. The absence of uncertainty estimation in learned models and their inability to account for the inherent ambiguity in decisions poses a major issue. This study proposes a new model called Indecision Forest, an adaptive and multi-strategy approach that incorporates two key concepts: quantified ambiguity, which enables a specified level of uncertain outcome prediction, and argument-based reasoning, which facilitates the incorporation of explicit justifications for decision-making. A novel learning scheme is developed to train Indecision Forest, which is demonstrated to be effective across various applications including decision-making under uncertainty, diffusion in social networks, and a realistic medical case study. The analysis shows that Indecision Forest strikes a balance between decision certainty and true uncertainty, thus making it an invaluable tool for tackling problems that are rooted in uncertain outcomes and diffusion processes. The DTW distance is a widely used measure in time series analysis but its efficiency is limited by its high time complexity, which can be mitigated by pruning and parallelization strategies. A recent approach, PrunedDTW, improves the DTW distance's time efficiency without sacrificing its accuracy, however its progress in reducing complexity is slow and does not completely fix the issue. Even with PrunedDTW, the majority of time is still spent on the last stages of the algorithm. We propose an enhanced version, early discarding PrunedDTW (EDPrunedDTW), which incorporates an additional decision to terminate the algorithm's remaining components early, thus significantly reducing the time complexity to O(N^2/2 + N) when considering all possible start points. EDPrunedDTW also has a constant memory footprint and is compatible with other pruning methods. Through an evaluation of nearest neighbor searches using synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that EDPrunedDTW achieves the best overall performance in terms of accuracy and computational performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of EDPrunedDTW in a similarity retrieval task on the UCR dominance dataset. EDPrunedDTW is now available as an open-source library for Python. It is also compatible with the AnomalyDetCTools library for efficient use in anomaly detection tasks. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/CalPolyAI/PrunedDTW. Software professionals require conceptual evaluation skills, which can be deficient in students graduating from computer science programs. Current teaching methods in software testing education focus on question-driven approaches to develop these skills within teaching environments. This study assesses the efficacy of two evaluation methods in software testing education: inquiry-based conceptual response and detailed evaluation. The latter method is commonly used, whereas the former involves having students provide a single sentence answer to a testing-related question posed in a real-world scenario. An experiment was conducted to compare the outcomes of these methods within a teaching setting. The results showed no statistically significant differences between the methods in terms of accuracy and feedback provided. However, the inquiry-based approach was found to be faster to grade and received higher satisfaction ratings from both students and the instructor. These findings indicate that the inquiry-based conceptual response method can be an effective alternative to traditional methods in software testing education. Future studies should aim to expand on these results by conducting studies outside of the university setting. Additionally, the characteristics of effective questions that foster conceptual evaluation skills within the inquiry-based approach were identified and discussed. They include a clear task description, sufficient context, and a well-defined answer option, which can serve as a basis for further research on how to teach these skills in software testing education. The code and data used in this study are publicly available for reproduction. Recommendations are also provided for practitioners on how to develop and use question sets that foster conceptual evaluation skills in software testing education. These claims can be validated by reviewing the data, which includes the used code and data. An action plan is proposed for software testing educators to incorporate the inquiry-based conceptual response method into their teaching practices, which may vary depending on the specific testing topic and question set used. The study's findings are intended to contribute to research on how to teach conceptual evaluation skills in software testing education. This research seeks to understand why deep neural networks (DNNs) make specific predictions by examining the intermediate results of three subsequent DNN layers. We use decision trees learned from selected input/output data to explain the reasoning behind these predictions, as decision trees are easily interpretable. However, decision trees can't capture the complex interactions present in high-dimensional data, and analyzing intermediate results is a labor-intensive task. To overcome these challenges, we develop a two-step approach, integrating concept analysis and inductive logic programming (ILP), to merge different decision trees generated from various datasets. This method enables us to pinpoint crucial features and map them to the network's layer parameters, thereby elucidating the decision trees' contributions to predicting specific outcomes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on both synthetic and real-world data, successfully merging multiple decision trees and identifying essential features to explain the decision trees' actions. Furthermore, we show that the network's layer parameters, along with the extracted features, allow us to create an ILP model that accurately predicts specific outcomes on unseen data. This breakthrough has potential applications in various fields, such as medicine and law, where data is frequently multi-dimensional and understanding the decision-making process is paramount. While our current findings only speak to what features a model is looking at, not its underlying structure, this research paves the way for future developments in explaining the decision-making processes of sophisticated machine learning models. It also lays the groundwork for future investigations into the underlying structures of these models. Ultimately, we believe this approach will enable organizations to better understand and justify the decisions made by the automated systems they interact with. Precise understanding of how a model operates could lead to significant cost savings resulting from decreased data annotation costs. This clarity could also increase trust in these automated systems since users would gain insight into the decision-making processes that ultimately affect them. This research is an extension of the author's doctoral thesis. This material is a revised and edited version of previously published research, specifically: "Explaining Intermediates and Layer Parameters in Deep Neural Networks through ILP," published in the 2022 IJCAI, and "Merging Concept Analysis with ILP to Pinpoint Crucial Features in Decision Trees," published in the 2022 ECMLPKDD. Additionally, this research is related to "From Decision Trees to ILP: Concept Analysis for Data Analysis and Explanation," published in the 2022 ECMLPKDD. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been effectively applied to
sparsely-connected datasets but we observe a significant decline in their
performance on densely-connected datasets, revealing an apparent limitation.
Upon closer examination, we find the primary issue to be over-blurring -
resulting from the fusion of adjacent nodes' features in the graph convolution
operation, which worsens on dense graphs where nodes are more interconnected.
To address this over-blurring, we propose a novel graph convolution operator
known as CrossGraph Convolution (CGC) that maintains feature distinctness.
Evaluations on various benchmarks demonstrate our method outperforms standard

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate identification of abnormal heart sounds is challenging even for experienced physicians due to the similarity of associated sounds and environmental interference.  Developing effective automatic cardiac auscultation systems is, therefore, a necessity.  Most current methods focus solely on distinct cardiac phases, overlooking the dynamic sound patterns produced by muscle contractions.  Furthermore, they fail to consider how environmental noises might affect the sounds.  Autoencoders have the potential to be adapted for cardiac auscultation by identifying a lower-dimensional representation from cardiac sound recordings.  By doing so, the inherent patterns within the data can be highlighted, and variations due to noise or source location can be accounted for.  In this research, we present an innovative approach to cardiac sound classification using an autoencoder-based model, one that incorporates the phase-dependent dynamics of heart sounds and is resilient to the effects of noise.  The study features a novel database of 2,082 heart sounds obtained from 208 subjects using digital stethoscopes in a clinical environment.  The database includes multiple abnormal murmur types and normal controls, recorded alongside various levels of background noise.  The method involves transforming the recorded sounds into time-frequency images through continuous Fourier transformation, and then transforming these into 2-dimensional representations through convolutional deformation.  These representations are then fed into a custom-designed autoencoder, which generates an embedded space used for classification.  The performance of the model was tested using 10-fold cross-validation, and compared with four separate baseline models, one of which was an ensemble of shallow networks trained on time-frequency images.  The results indicate that our approach produces a classification accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score of 88%, 81%, 94%, and 0.87 respectively.  In comparison, the baseline model achieved accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score of 82%, 68%, 92%, and 0.84 for deep networks working directly with time-frequency images.  Consequently, the proposed method has enhanced its effectiveness by focusing on extracting relevant cardiac sound features through both phase-dependent dynamics and a resilient encoding strategy.  The study's code and database are available for public access at https://github.com/ashkanzangeneh/Cardiac_Auscultation. We identify a necessary and sufficient condition for the fractional sequence operator to be bounded within these spaces. Additionally, this study examines the essential spectrum, spectrum, and eigenvalues of the fractional sequence operator within the discrete $H_p^($ space for $1 < p < 2$, and we derive a key finding regarding the existence of eigenvalues. Moreover, this research introduces new techniques for solving the operator equation $\sum_{n=m}^{\infty} a_n \tau^n f = \sum_{n=m}^{\infty} b_n \tau^n f$ in the context of bounded linear operators within the context of $H_2^($. The solutions obtained in this research are expressed in terms of mathematical functions defined on the forward orbit $\{\omega, \omega^2, \omega^3, \dots\}$, where $\omega$ represents the common ratio of the sequence $\{1, \tau, \tau^2, \dots\}$. We relate the solutions obtained in this research to the concept of Abel summation and its extension, but unlike previous studies, this research demonstrates that the solutions can exist universally under specific conditions for singular operators within the given spaces. This study offers an initial examination of trustworthiness in a second-price auction setting. Our model encompasses a wide range of trust mechanisms inherent in these auctions, allowing for the evaluation of their individual effect. We discovered a significant reduction in trustworthiness with the introduction of a trusted third-party mechanism, which did not demonstrate a notable difference in revenue compared to a traditional auction. Our findings also highlighted a sizeable decrease in bid variability with the introduction of trustworthiness. We proposed a new auction design, leveraging a trustworthiness interval rather than a single bid, which showed promise in an empirical setting. This auction displayed improved price accuracy and reduced bid variability. Our theoretical analysis quantified the benefits of this design. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of trustworthiness in auctions and introduces an innovative auction mechanism that effectively leverages trustworthiness to achieve superior outcomes. 

Note that this research was influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic, which restricted access to physical experiments. As a result, we could only conduct a small, online trial with a relatively low number of participants. We are exploring physical and additional field experiments to validate our findings further. 

For the purpose of completeness, we are providing the detailed report on this study in the attached document.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology's emergence has been a primary focus in modern cosmology.  A novel theory of modified gravity, known as $f(Q)$-gravity, has been proposed as a possible explanation for this phenomenon.  The theory involves gravity's cyclic nature, a concept that has sparked significant interest.  A specific class of locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi-I universes based on this theory is examined in this study.  The acceleration of these universes is closely linked to complex interplay between matter and gravitational effects, a phenomenon that is unique to this type of modified gravity.  A general condition for this theory is that an average acceleration may arise due to non-minimal interaction between matter and gravitational fields, a phenomenon that can be observed in the theory's action integral.  Furthermore, this study demonstrates that both accelerated and decelerated cosmological expansion can be supported by this theory, a finding that is consistent with experimental data.  A particular model of $f(Q)$-gravity is analyzed in detail, and the study shows that this theory can lead to a universe with rotationally symmetric structures in certain scenarios.  The findings of this research are relevant to the theory of cyclic gravity, a novel approach to understanding the origin of cosmological acceleration.  A comparison of this theory's predictions to observational data is also presented in this study.  The data shows that a universally applicable model of $f(Q)$-gravity with pure cosmological constant type parameter exhibits the best fit with observational data.  A wide range of locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi-I universes based on this theory is then examined in this study.  The results reveal that these theories are conducive to a universe with rotationally symmetric structures in certain types of cosmological scenarios, a phenomenon that is unique to these types of modified gravity.  The study also shows that both accelerated and decelerated cosmological expansion can be supported by these theories, and that a universally applicable model of $f(Q)$-gravity with a cosinearch parameter is the best fit with observational data.  A significant finding of this research is that a cyclic type $f(Q)$-gravity may arise due to non-minimal interaction between matter and gravitational fields, a phenomenon that is observable in the theory's action integral. Within the context of a minimal vector-like extension that accounts for the new $Z'$ gauge boson, we analyze how the $K^+e^-$ anomaly and the $K/\pi$ anomaly, as well as $b\rightarrow s$ anomalies, are concurrently resolved. Our research demonstrates that a minimal vector-like composite operator can explain all observed anomalies, resulting in a mass for the $Z'$ gauge boson that falls in the $4.1-\cup 5.1$ GeV range. In order to accomplish a wide range of information-related tasks both professionally and personally, individuals must first become informed about relevant existing knowledge and then locate the appropriate sources.  The process of acquiring this knowledge is often referreded to as information seeking behavior (ISB).  ISB can take many forms, such as seeking fact-based information for a specific purpose or seeking diverse forms of social interaction.  This paper presents a comprehensive study of ISB characterized by a high level of purposefulness and social interaction in a community setting.  Researchers have developed a standardized questionnaire to investigate the nature of information seeking behavior in everyday life: the Information Seeking Behavior Questionnaire (ISBQ).  Through a multi-step process, researchers used the ISBQ to analyze the content of 201 responses from a sample of research participants.  The results show that individuals seek information on numerous topics, including how to access useful information and how to interact with others during information seeking.  This study is significant because it provides a comprehensive understanding of ISB that includes a wide range of purposeful and socially oriented behavior and identifies specific areas of need in information seeking behavior that has not been previously addressed.  Furthermore, the results can be utilized to further refine existing theories and guidelines in information seeking behavior, potentially leading to more effective information seeking practices in the future.  In addition, the paper presents a series of recommendations that information providers can implement to better meet the diverse information needs of their users.  Finally, the paper presents a series of research questions that will guide future research in the field of information seeking behavior. (2017) and Wilson et al. (2019). By incorporating the full spectrum of neutrinos and neutrons, the models in this study accurately predict the development of instabilities, unlike previous two-dimensional models. The results show that a flavor instability initially develops along a narrow axis in the innermost region of the supernova, leading to the creation of neutrino "clumps" that can potentially influence the overall shape of the neutrino output. The growth rate of these instabilities is highest when they occur in regions with the highest neutrino densities, and is largely unaffected by variations in electron-neutrino muon-neutrino ratio. The models also suggest that a secondary instability can develop due to the interaction of neutrinos with each other, rather than simply axis-related effects. ADHD is characterized by a range of symptoms including difficulty paying attention to the point of neglecting things, excessive impulsive behavior, and lowered ability to concentrate. Advances in computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence have significantly improved diagnosis accuracy rates for ADHD since its initial identification as a disorder in the late 19th century. Recent breakthroughs in computational capabilities and machine learning methods, in particular, have led to significant progress in this field. Rational brain region selection for ADHD analysis has been a major component of computational diagnosing efforts, which often rely on resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). This technique measures the brain's activity while it is at rest, which is essential for understanding linked brain regions and systems. We conducted a comprehensive study to determine the effectiveness of using essential regions of the brain for diagnosing ADHD through deep learning without any preconceptions. This study involved selecting crucial regions of the brain based on information extracted from rs-fMRI data for both diagnostic and non-diagnostic groups. This dataset was then used to train and validate a deep learning model based on convolutional neural networks (CNN). In our investigation, we explore an epidemic SISI model where individuals interact with each other at specific times and assume an infectious status is variable. The aim of this study is to analyze the distinct-time epidemic SISI model's long-term effects on a population, specifically how the model responds to variations in time intervals between individual interactions and periods of infectiousness. These long-term effects are examined through the use of a mathematical formula, known as the Epidemic Equilibrium distribution, which allows us to make comparisons with existing literature and draw inferences about the critical threshold in dynamic models. This analysis not only enhances our understanding of how long-term epidemics evolve but also sheds light on the importance of accurately measuring the critical threshold in complex systems. The findings of this research are further illustrated through numerical solutions to a corresponding differential equation that represents the rate of change in epidemic size over time, specifically in a population of 10 individuals. These simulations not only confirm our earlier findings but also reveal more general truths about population dynamics. One notable discovery from our research is that the shape of the Epidemic Equilibrium distribution is solely dependent on the specific characteristics of individual interactions, whereas the rate of change in epidemic size over time is influenced by multiple factors, including interaction patterns and periods of infectiousness. The significant contributions of this study stem from our detailed analysis of distinct-time models, particularly our results showing that even brief contact periods can lead to long-term epidemics and that there exists a critical threshold for the probability of infection that dictates whether or not an epidemic will occur. These key findings provide valuable insights into the crucial roles that contact duration and the probability of infection play in determining the outcome and long-term effects of an epidemic. Additionally, our research reveals the crucial role that monitoring and tracking individual interactions could play in predicting the outcome and long-term effects of an epidemic, particularly in environments where there is a high volume of interactions occurring over extended periods of time. The substantial advancements made by this study lay the groundwork for further exploration into the broad applicability of distinct-time models in studying the behavior and dynamics of complex populations. Specifically, we propose that our approach should be applied in the analysis of phenomena that involve periodic or irregular interactions among individuals, such as the scheduling of classes or the occurrence of random events. Furthermore, we suggest that our results could be utilized in developing strategies for disease control and epidemic prevention, particularly in environments where there is limited access to information about individual interactions. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are integral to concise writing, they can also introduce confusion if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unfamiliar to the reader. To address this issue, this paper introduces MadDog, a comprehensive system designed to identify and clarify acronym ambiguities within given texts. MadDog's process involves two key components: improving dataset quality and enhancing computational algorithms. For the former, the system seeks human input to update existing datasets, leveraging two distinct approaches - crowdsourcing and expert knowledge. Once revised, the updated datasets are utilized to train Machine Learning models, which are subsequently integrated with the system to deliver accurate acronym definitions and related phrases upon user input. To gauge the efficacy of our methods, the research includes an examination of MadDog's performance using standard evaluation metrics as well as a comparative analysis with existing, comparable systems. Our results indicate that MadDog significantly enhances acronym recognition accuracy across various domains and demonstrate the system's capacity for large-scale, real-time acronym analysis through an online demo available at [www.acronycs.com](http://www.acronycs.com). MadDog's code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/acronycs/MadDog. Additionally, a demo of the system is available at www.acronycs.com. The system's code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/acronycs/MadDog. The acronym definitions dataset used in this research is known as AcronymCS and can be accessed via this link: https://github.com/acronycs/AcronymCS. It is worth noting that MadDog is an open-source revision of the AcronymCS platform, which was initially presented in the study titled "AcronymCS: a Large-Scale Acronym Dataset for English," published in the Proceedings of the International Conference on Big Data, BilbaO18. The revised system reflects valuable feedback and suggestions from IJERnC, which led to significant enhancements and improvements in accuracy. The updated MadDog system represents a more robust version of AcronymCS, featuring updated datasets and revised algorithms. The research includes an examination of MadDog's performance, its comparison with other similar systems, such as WikiAbbrev, and a demonstration of the system's capacity for large-scale, real-time acronym analysis through an online demo available at www.acronycs.com. The code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/acronycs/MadDog.

By integrating cache managers, we achieve a significant reduction in data requests and mutations, making the storage more efficient and scalable. Our experimental results show that these additions lead to a substantial decrease in data refresher traffic and improve read throughput in test files. Our approach provides the best performance in read throughput among all options, while also minimizing additional overhead and making the storage accessible to a broader range of devices. Topological momentum structures can be characterized through topological invariants, which remain unchanged under system transformations preserving momentum space symmetry. This concept has been successfully incorporated into designing momentum manipulators and optical systems. A key feature of these invariants is their chiral and non-chiral nature, which has been leveraged in creating devices manipulating momentum and applying this concept to optical systems. However, there is a lack of a comprehensive overview on this subject, limiting the integration of concepts from momentum-space topology to the quantum optics community. This introduction provides an accessible understanding of momentum-space topology and its applications to photonic systems. It discusses the practical uses of topological invariants, distinguishes between chiral and non-chiral modes, and explores recent advancements in the control of momentum in photonic systems. Furthermore, the potential future applications and extensions of momentum-space topology are considered, with possibilities including the use of Frenkel excitons in organic materials and the development of new techniques for optical imaging and sensing. By bringing together research on photonic systems and solid-state physics, momentum-space topology can be advanced, leading to new breakthroughs in the field. In oscillatory medium environments, pacemaker-generated waves can be observed to transmit steadily over extended distances in time, frequently utilized in various biological systems such as biological neurons and muscle cells for signal conduction.  This article explores the exponential model proposed by Krogh et al. in 1993 for describing the velocity of traveling waves generated by pacemaker activity, specifically in the context of Lee "hole-in-one" model for biological neuron propagation and related spatial activation scenarios.  By applying numerical and analytical methods, we evaluate the influence of spatial nonlinearity and pacemaker dynamics on wave propagation, revealing that the model produces accurate velocity predictions across a wide range of parameters, thus validating the 1993 model's effectiveness.  This model's potential applications extend to understanding and modeling various biological systems as well as fluid dynamics phenomena involving triggered wave processes.

In this article we examine the exponential model proposed in 1993 for describing velocities of traveling waves generated by pacemaker activity, specifically in the context of Lee 'hole-in-one' model and related spatial activation scenarios.  The model predicts that velocities of these waves are dependent on the ratio of their frequency to the decay rate of the medium's oscillatory properties.  We investigate this model's applicability to a wide range of parameters, specifically pacemaker dynamics and spatial nonlinearity, using numerical and analytical methods.  The results of these investigations confirm that the model produces accurate velocity predictions across a wide range of parameters, thus validating the 1993 model's effectiveness.  We explore the implications of the model in understanding and modeling both biological systems and fluid dynamics phenomena involving triggered wave processes.  We provide public code and figures to replicate our results, allowing for further reproduction and analysis

We have developed two novel algorithms for approximating the von Neumann entropy (NE) that use only a small number of quantum operations: one generalized algorithm and one optimized variant, tailored for near-classical computing with classical post-processing. Both algorithms work by randomly partitioning the NE into sections, then utilizing local properties of the density matrix to achieve their goals. Our empirical results show that the optimized variant exhibits exponential convergence in approximation errors, using significantly fewer quantum operations than expectation-value estimation methods. These algorithms may find practical use in near-classical computing and quantum simulation environments where resource limitations apply. Our source code is available at https://github.com/qiskit/algorithm/blob/d9b7f9e9a443cee1b0da4d1e8b8f9a9qiskit_terra/blob/master/quantum_info/entropy.py. It is established that these ideals have at most one codimension one defect and are elicited by squaring a particular type of monomial ideal, referred to as strongly persistently linear. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the codimension of this squared ideal is less than the squared codimension of the original ideal. In the case of bipartite graph encoding monomial ideals, it is observed that nearly Cohen-Macaulay property and this specific squared ideal property are equivalent to a specific graph condition. Examples and coexistence pairs of monomial ideals are also provided to illustrate the distinct nature of this class of ideals, including one instance where the ideal has two codimension one defects. Further study on this class of ideals is suggested.

Real-time, screen-space shadow rendering has a significant influence on a scene's overall appearance but suffers from limitations, including inaccurate bounding volume overlap detection and inability to support texture shading. These restrictions make it unsuitable for inverse problems such as solving Poisson problems and generating image-based lighting. This paper introduces an alternative screen-space shadow method that overcomes these hurdles by employing a voxelized bounding volume overlap detection that can be differentiated and uses a unique image space average depth map technique. This new method not only enhances shadow quality but also facilitates image-based lighting. Multiple implementations have demonstrated the efficiency and reliability of this approach. Furthermore, it has been successfully used in the real-time rendering of a highly detailed and textured game environment called "Cyberpunk 2077." We confidently assert that our screen-space shadow method is the best available solution, especially for gaming applications. A publicly accessible code repository is available for this work at the address https://github.com/CNRLab/Cyberpunk2077SSS. A video showcasing the paper's methods and results is available at the address https://youtu.be/LOcX_cCp4Gk. We would like to extend our appreciation to the editors, reviewers, and our colleagues for their support and feedback. We also wish to acknowledge the financial support of a CNR research fund. We used the Unreal Engine 4 as a platform for this work to achieve a much faster development cycle, utilizing its built-in features whenever possible to minimize research overhead. We leveraged Unreal Engine 4's modular architecture to introduce our new screen-space shadow method, isolating our modifications in a customizable module for widespread use. This approach allowed us to integrate our new shadow method with other third-party modules and maintain a clean, consistent code base. We used Cyberpunk 2077 as a test case to validate our screen-space shadow method, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency in a real-world, in-game scenario. Cyberpunk 2077 is known for its highly detailed and rich environments, which presented complex bounding volume overlap detection issues. We successfully overcome these challenges, achieving superior shadow quality. We also applied our new shadow method to solve Poisson problems and generate image-based lighting, resulting in a 5% increase in target variables. We used various metrics to evaluate our screen-space shadow method, including a novel direction-based error metric. This error metric is based on a vector field and can be used to quantify shadow accuracy. We demonstrated the efficiency of our screen-space shadow method through a memory usage analysis, which showed a substantial reduction in memory

Transportation managers regularly make decisions that affect traffic flow, but the unpredictable nature of traffic patterns makes it difficult to generate accurate predictions. By utilizing recent traffic data and incorporating statistical analysis, the objective of this study is to establish the probabilistic origin-destination demands for a network. A mathematical framework is developed to define origin-destination demands and their associated probabilities, followed by a statistical approach to estimate these demands. This approach is tested on a small sample size and compared with existing methods, including a frequentist analysis based on observed traffic data and a model that incorporates zone-specific traffic patterns. Results indicate that the proposed statistical method performs similarly to other methods, but this approach offers more transparent and reliable traffic demand estimates that can be utilized for statistical inference. Ultimately, the study demonstrates how daily traffic data can inform the understanding of origin-destination demands and support statistical inference. A case study in the Mexico City metro area highlights the applicability of this approach in a real-world setting. Current research focuses on utilizing these probabilities for statistical inference, such as identifying unusual demand patterns or comparing the traffic patterns of two zones. Future research aims to expand upon these ideas, in addition to utilizing the proposed demands for traffic forecasting and management decisions. The proposed methodology is available on GitHub for public access. The empirical results from the Mexico City metro area can be found in an accompanying notebook on GitHub. The necessary data for this project can be obtained through an application process with ITDP. A detailed guide on replicating the results and the necessary code can be found on the study's website. Several limitations hinder the widespread adoption of this approach, primarily stemming from the need for sufficient daily traffic data and zone-specific traffic patterns. The frequency of daily traffic data affects the accuracy of the proposed probabilistic origin-destination demands, with lower frequencies resulting in less accurate estimates. When the daily traffic data is insufficient, the proposed approach struggles to generate accurate results. Another critical challenge is determining the appropriate sample size for the origin-destination matrix. When the matrix is sparse, the frequency of daily traffic patterns is inherently limited, but a larger sample size is required to account for the greater number of unique origin-destination pairs. In contrast, when the matrix is dense, the frequency of daily traffic patterns is higher, but a smaller sample size is preferred due to the reduced complexity of the origin-destination matrix. In interconnecting regular arrays of oscillators featuring diverse behaviors, synchronization patterns beyond the traditional phase-locking type have been observed. Although the dynamics of the oscillators may differ greatly, they often exhibit intricate order and sync patterns were found to emerge through multiple routes of formation. By utilizing numerical simulations and further validated with experiments in coupled semiconductor lasers, our study reveals how the diversity of the oscillators affects the resulting synchronized states. We've observed a higher structural complexity in the synchronized states with increased diversity. Moreover, the time it takes for the synchronization to occur decreases with the degree of diversity. Our findings provide new insights into how complex systems can maintain functional order despite uncertainty. They also open up possibilities for diverse oscillator systems to be used in designing robust clocks that can operate accurately despite irregular timing inputs or for applications where functional order is prioritized over regular timing. Lastly, our research paves the way for further exploration into how dynamic systems can maintain their physiological function despite systemic instability. It also offers possibilities for diverse oscillator systems to be used in designing clocks that can operate accurately despite irregular timing inputs or for applications where functional order is prioritized over regular timing. We propose an approach to achieve this through feedback mechanisms that could potentially lead to new technologies for secure data transmission and bio-medical applications. It also offers a model to study and understand how living organisms can maintain their functional order despite systemic instability. We demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve functional order while allowing for diversity in the system, thus challenging the long-standing premise that regular timing is necessary for functional order. Furthermore, we reveal that a high level of structural complexity in the system can maintain its functional order even when individual components exhibit chaotic behavior. We establish a relationship between the system's structural properties and its dynamic behavior, and demonstrate how numerical simulations can be validated with experiments in order to better understand natural phenomena. Additionally, we propose a novel design for optical clock systems that could operate reliably even under harsh conditions due to their diversity-based design. It is an innovative concept that could be adaptable to various technological applications where functional order is crucial and regular timing is not necessary. Lastly, we show that our research offers a new theoretical framework for understanding and studying complex systems that could be used to inform future research in physics, by identifying the underlying principles of organization in diverse oscillator systems and how these principles could be applied to other areas of physics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our research in oscillator arrays could be applied to other domains such as neuroscience, by uncovering the diverse oscillator mechanisms that underpin brain function and enabling novel therapeutic approaches.

We're investigating the behavior of dark solitons in the mean-field equation of the Gross-Pitaevskii type, taking into account the influence of non-linear change in dispersion. Our research reveals that, unlike what happens with linear change in dispersion, the mean-field theory predicts an increase in the energy associated with a dark soliton as its width decreases when there's a negative non-linear dispersion. This leads us to explore the effect at the one-dimensional level using finite-range fermiization and strong-dispersion perturbation theory. Our results show that, contrary to predictions from mean-field theories, solitons with negative non-linear dispersion not only maintain their stability but also exhibit an energy minimum at a moderately narrow width. Moreover, we expand our research to the two-dimensional case, analyzing planar and radial scenarios separately. Our findings suggest that, only in radial scenarios with a sufficient number of atoms, solitons exhibit an energy minimum at a moderately narrow width. Our research provides theoretical evidence to support recent experimental observations, explaining the occurrence of soliton formation and stability in the presence of non-linear change in dispersion. It also sheds light on underlying mechanics, revealing that radius acts as a stabilizing factor, which is a counter-intuitive conclusion when considering mean-field theories. To further deepen our understanding, we analyzed the impact of non-thermalization in fermiization, discovering that it contributes to soliton stability in scenarios with strong non-linear change in dispersion. Our research indicates that, only in cases with small non-linear change in dispersion, perturbation theory and mean-field theories at both one and two dimensions yield similar results and predict soliton instability. Our predictions made with strong-dispersion perturbation theory match experimental outcomes, providing a scale for measuring non-linear change in dispersion that separates stable and unstable dark solitons. Our research has far-reaching implications, paving the way for soliton creation and stability in numerous optical media, such as BECs (bosonic-liquid elements) and optical fibers. It also encourages future research on the role of non-thermalization in describing soliton behavior. Direction is a crucial concept in visual analytics but remains poorly defined, which hindering seamless communication between human researchers and machine learning algorithms. Existing approaches to direction are either too narrow or too vague, unable to be applied in a practical setting. We introduce Lotse, a structure consisting of foundational elements to define direction, by combining spatial and orientational components, allowing for an extensive interpretation and broad generalizability. The framework is now accessible in an open-source format on GitHub. Further development is welcomed through contributions and feedback.

Despite the availability of various algorithms for solving these systems, obtaining efficient solutions in terms of memory and computation becomes a significant challenge when dealing with larger problem sizes.  Although multilevel methods have shown potential in dealing with larger problems, they often lack a fundamental explanation of their effectiveness.  In this study, we compare the performance of various multilevel algorithms used for cardiac mechanics in terms of execution time and memory consumption.  Our evaluation is conducted using a range of problem sizes from 275K to 13.8M unknowns.  Besides testing different multilevel conditions, we also experimented with approximating conditions and delaying the computation of one-level systems.  Our findings demonstrate that these techniques lead to substantial reductions in memory requirements, at the cost of slightly increased solution times.  Ultimately, we observe a direct proportionality between problem size and solution time.  It is noteworthy that all of these techniques result in comparable time and memory performance, underscoring the importance of systematic algorithmic analysis to identify the best strategy for a specific application.  In addition to these numerical experiments, we have also implemented and demonstrated the composition of two multilevel algorithms, showcasing their capacity to solve coupled problems in cardiac mechanics.  This research is part of a broader effort to develop and use advanced algorithms for coupled problems in biological mechanics, a field with vast theoretical and applied potential.  This work may also have far-reaching implications for other fields such as cardiovascular medicine.  Our algorithms can be reproduced using an active branch of the deal.II module deal.II_coupledMechBiol Mechanics and an independent module deal.II_conditioning. We plan to publicly release our code and demonstrate the mentioned applications in the near future. Long-lived reinforcement learning agents automatically adapt to achieve their best performance over an extended period. This adaptation is referred to as lifelong reinforcement learning. Despite the importance of evaluating these agents, current methods have several drawbacks as they: 1) primarily rely on simulated environments with limited scenarios, 2) do not assess performance across various tasks, 3) lack a direct comparison with traditional agents, and 4) underestimate the dependence of lifelong reinforcement learning methods on data from other sources. We introduce an evaluation framework called L2Explorer, set in a virtual 3D world, where agents navigate and adapt through an ever-changing sequence of interconnected tasks over an indefinite period. This platform resembles a real-world environment by incorporating diverse aspects such as dynamic goal changes, partially observable spaces, and unpredictable movements. Our analysis using four benchmark models demonstrates that L2Explorer successfully assesses the performance of lifelong reinforcement learning methods and highlights their limitations when applied in a dynamic and goal-shifting environment. We observed significant variations in performance across different goal changes for all the benchmark models and found that three of these models performed similarly to random navigation but slightly better in static environments with predefined objectives. This study's findings indicate that existing lifelong reinforcement learning methods are not adequate in responsive and adaptive scenarios, and thus more research is needed to develop effective strategies. We launched an online challenge based on L2Explorer, and the latest results can be found on our website at https://l2explorer.github.io/. We welcome the reinforcement learning community to participate and further improve our understanding of lifelong reinforcement learning by using L2Explorer. In our study, we explored four benchmark models. Three of these were by Stella et al. using RNNs and a policy network, and one was an MDP model. We found that all of these performed similarly to random navigation but slightly better in static environments with predefined objectives. Moreover, we discovered that two of these models could adapt to new objectives in a partial observable setting but struggled in other situations. We found that one of these models was sensitive to data from other sources and performed poorly when data was limited. Additionally, we observed that one of these models performed poorly when goals changed frequently but responded positively to changes in a more gradual, natural environment. We found that another model performed well across a wide range of goals but was less effective in a partial observable setting and required a large amount of data to adapt to new objectives. They initially contract and then expand, with their motion governed by a non-local equation. These solutions represent a novel type of wave solutions and have important implications in understanding certain statistical models and micro-scale turbulence phenomena. When the background flow is perturbed, these solutions can serve as initial conditions, which are then repelled away from the perturbation. This behavior has potential applications in understanding perturbed shearing flows observed in various natural phenomena and numerical simulations. Furthermore, these solutions can be extended to the Euler equation's quasigeostrophic reduction model, which shares many similarities with the 2D Euler equation under certain conditions. For the quasigeostrophic equation, these solutions can be generalized even when the background flow's vorticity has singularities. In the case of weak background flow, these solutions can be derived without relying on Taylor-Couette flow assumptions, which are highly localized and have important implications in understanding various natural phenomena such as jet dynamics and the interaction between counter-rotating vortices. Lastly, these solutions can also be found in other hydrodynamic models, which may include the use of the Ginzburg-Landau equation's near-singularities.
