Large-scale online services rely heavily on information networks, which underlie various online platforms, enabling them to store user-generated content and connect entities. Effective management of data stored within these networks requires sophisticated structural analysis, which current research largely overlooks in favor of flat data management approaches. To fill this gap, our proposal focuses on developing a practical method for extracting network substructures on a large scale. Building upon existing algorithms, we've adapted and combined three known algorithms suitable for distributed computation and tested them across seven diverse datasets. Our comprehensive evaluation includes an in-depth analysis of the computational processes, a detailed examination of the extracted structures, and a comparison of the results to their corresponding single-machine implementations. Our tests demonstrate that our frameworks can efficiently handle large-scale networks, while also highlighting areas for further improvement. To facilitate reproducibility, we've made the source code and dataset descriptions publicly available. In the future, we plan to expand our frameworks to encompass additional structural properties and algorithmic enhancements. Additionally, we intend to explore applications of scalable structural analysis in machine learning and information retrieval within online services. With these initiatives, we aim to enhance the technical foundations of scalable structural analysis and promote its practical adoption in real-world online services. To showcase the feasibility of scalable structural analysis, we've presented a conceptual design for a companion system, which could significantly benefit from this approach. Specifically, we've outlined a plan for automatically generating search queries based on network substructures, which we've verified through a basic prototype and are interested in developing further. This proposed feature, built on scalable structural analysis, has the potential to significantly improve query quality and reduce reliance on pre-defined queries or limited manual extraction. We conducted an extensive study to verify the accuracy of the flux-based statistical prediction model for the three-body problem. This involved tracking over a thousand simulations of different eras from the Late Heavy Shell Era to the Late Heavy Shell Era with the presence of both large and tiny mass disparities. The results showed that the flux-based model performed exceptionally well, predicting lifetimes and orbital distances with great precision. Furthermore, we discovered that the model successfully captured the influence of several critical elements, including the Late Heavy Shell Period, the Equal Masses Boundary, and the scales of mass variations, all within a single set of pre-defined parameters. The excellent outcome of our tests supports the use of the flux-based model as a reliable tool for forecasting three-body systems. The findings of our research are documented in detailed reports and visualizations, as well as a comprehensive guide that includes all necessary formulas and technical details of the simulation protocol. This research will soon be published in a peer-reviewed article. The source code of our simulation tool has already been made publicly available on GitHub, while the visualizations and data are available on Zenodo. We are also planning to share the individual results in databases. Finally, the final section of our research is a forecast of how the flux-based model will perform in future astronomical studies. The forecast is based on our earlier work on the long-term evolution of the three-body problem. The predictions indicate that the flux-based model will accurately forecast specific properties of four-body and higher systems over vast timescales, all based on the model's performance in our previous study. The predictions were made by applying the model to a set of random outcomes from our simulations, and then analyzing the results over extremely long timescales. The precision of the model in these predictions is remarkably high, with great agreement between the forecast and the actual results. The key challenge here is the immense timescales involved, where the effects of rounding errors in the algorithm is most pronounced. The excellent outcome of our tests supports the use of the flux-based model as a reliable tool for forecasting long-term three-body and higher systems. The predictions made here may pave the way for future research in long-term astronomical studies, and could have significant practical applications in future endeavors. The timescales involved here are comparable to the long-term evolutionary timescales observed in stars, planets, and other celestial objects over extremely long ages, often exceeding millions of years. The flux-based model has successfully demonstrated its precision and accuracy in these timescales, and we believe it will similarly perform exceptionally well in the long-term evolutionary studies of celestial objects

We propose an extension to continuous logic currently used in topos theory, by adapting duality theory developed for commutative ring theory. This extension maintains the existing meaning of terms and formulas while introducing a new notion of equality. This revised framework is consistent with the initial formulation of continuous logic and allows us to define a category based on continuous models and morphisms between them. This category is demonstrated to have a dual structure and a set of logics that satisfy specific axioms forms a subcategory within it. Furthermore, we define a category of continuous categories and show that it is equivalent to another category for continuous logic initially presented by Fourman and sheaf topos theory, thus establishing a coherent whole for continuous logic. This whole can serve as a unifying framework for topos theory, sheaf theory, and continuous logic. Finally, we outline potential applications and areas for further investigation within continuous logic. One such area is model theory where an alternative approach to continuous logic could lead to significant discoveries. Specifically, the category we defined might provide a unified understanding of extended real numbers and enable research into categorical model theory for partial orders. Additionally, we suggest examining Mizar, a computer system that supports proof development in mathematical domains, and specifically the part related to topos theory and sheaf theory, to better integrate continuous logic contributions. Last but not least, we explore the connection between continuous logic and algebraic geometry through the category of continuous categories. This relationship could facilitate the transfer of knowledge between these two areas. Finally, we propose studying partial orders within the framework of categorical logic to reveal new insights. Suicidal individuals leave behind tragic memories for their loved ones. Identifying those who will attempt suicide is extremely crucial. Recent studies have the potential to transform this challenging task by combining various data sources, leveraging machine learning algorithms to detect suicidal individuals. Our research builds upon the successful approach of using deep learning sequences, specifically applying it to time-series data from electroencephalograms and text comments, to predict individuals who will attempt suicide. We've developed a novel deep learning model, the Suicidal Thoughts Sequence Network (STS-N), to tackle this critical task. The state-of-the-art method was initially tested and confirmed on the JUICER dataset and subsequent experiments involved combining EEG and text data to predict suicidal intentions, a complex multi-modal data analysis problem. The proposed model demonstrated exceptional results, achieving 0.944 AUC on the combined dataset, outperforming other methods by a substantial margin. Moreover, our study highlights the significant predictive value of integrating EEG and text data in identifying suicidal individuals, opening new avenues for utilizing multi-modal data in detecting suicidal risks. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub for others to build upon our research. We hope our approach will contribute to saving more lives by accurately identifying those at risk of suicide. We encourage fellow researchers to build upon our work, potentially using our approach as a baseline for future suicidal intention prediction studies. Obviously, there are infinitely many such sums if we allow values up to $n$ for any number of integers. However, we find that certain restrictions on the number of integers can still yield an infinite number of unique sums, regardless of the maximum value of the integers used. More specifically, we demonstrate that under these constraints, there are always at least $2^{n-1}$ such sums, matching an earlier proven result for combinations by Matvey Pavlov. The sound speed in dense matter is an essential concept in understanding density-driven stellar evolution and core-collapse supernovae using astrophysical neutrino oscillation parameters. We defined the sound speed as the speed of entropic waves in the MIT-bags equation and obtained its expression in dense stellar matter consisting of nucleons, neutrons, protons, and various strange hadrons. By numerically analyzing the properties of strange stars made of this matter, we found that the sound speed decreases rapidly within the core and increases gradually towards the star's surface. These results show that the presence of strange quarks affects the sound speed and its gradient in the core and outer layers of strange stars, leading to a different behavior compared to neutron stars. Additionally, we found that the kaonless matter's sound speed is always lower than its kaon-present counterpart, particularly in the outer layers of the star. These findings are consistent across various different bag energies and chemical potentials. They may help explain the recently discovered, extremely dense star PSR Jaxa 0738+3132, which has a radius of only 10 km and a mass of about 2.17 solar masses. The sound speeds we found could be useful in future neutron star and strange star seismology. They also provide parameters for studying core-collapse supernovae using astrophysical neutrino oscillation parameters in dense stellar matter. Finally, these results may help deepen our understanding of the dense nuclear matter that constitutes the core of neutron stars and strange stars. If confirmed by future seismic measurements, these results may shed new light on the dense nuclear matter that these compact stars are made of. We investigate a variety of states that can be generated through dual-jump processes, specifically examining how squeezing affects a state when a coherent amplitude is introduced. Typically, squeezing transforms a coherent state into a Laguerre polynomial series. However, our analysis shows that when a dual-jump process is applied to a Laguerre polynomial series with non-zero coherent amplitude, the resulting state cannot be represented by a Laguerre polynomial series. Instead, we derive a new expression for the probability distribution of the quantum field operator in terms of Fock states. Additionally, we demonstrate that the influence of squeezing on the coherent amplitude is not uniform, but rather varies depending on the specific order of squeezing and tonicino operations, corresponding to dual-jump processes. Specifically, applying squeezing first leads to a discrete, doubly periodic pattern in the state's probability distribution, whereas tonicino operations yield a continuously periodic pattern. Our findings also highlight a limitation in using certain classical field-theoretic models that assume a continuous, periodic state probability distribution, revealing a discrepancy between these models and quantum field theory predictions at low frequencies (i.e., "deep in the infrared"). Lastly, we discuss how our dual-jump approach to modeling quantum field theories may provide insight into phenomena involving "supra-thermal" or "negative" phonon behavior. This approach could also be adapted to study other complex systems that are driven by competing mechanisms. Further exploration of this method could reveal additional connections between quantum field theory and systems exhibiting supra-thermal phenomena. To validate our predictions, we have prepared a publicly available code in Mathematica that can generate dual-jump evolution tables for any combination of unitary operators and initial states. This code is capable of efficiently computing scale-invariant properties even for extremely large quantum fields, achieving a degree of numerical precision on the order of 10^-16. We also employed it to study other forms of dual-jump evolution that are grounded in physical principles such as the $p$-adic action of Tonicino operators. We were able to verify that our predictions for both coherent and compress states align with the findings of prior quantum field theory studies. We found that the compress state's probability distribution exhibits symmetry under a transformation that is equivalent to a combination of left and right shifts of the Fock state basis. This symmetry is not limited to a specific range of phonon number; rather, it persists across the entire Fock space. During gas-liquid two-phase flows, the relative volume occupied by the phases changes, resulting in fluid interfaces with intricate geometries that affect the flow's physical properties. For instance, when simulating three-dimensional fluid dynamics, the interfaces can be represented by surfaces that are difficult to analyze directly due to their complex nature. Therefore, in this work, we propose the use of interface skeletons as a tool for studying multiphase flow architectures. The skeletonization process creates a network from the interfaces, allowing for the investigation of the flow's physical characteristics. We introduce several metrics to characterize the skeletally represented interfaces and demonstrate their effectiveness on a model system of gas jets penetrating liquid droplets. These metrics encompass both global parameters, such as network statistics and mass distribution analysis, and local indicators, like branch length distributions and branch influence metrics. Our study shows that these methods are capable of mapping the evolution of the flow's architecture from the interfaces to its underlying skeleton, and are versatile for applying in various types of multiphase flows. The implementation details of our technique are available online for other researchers to use. Furthermore, we suggest multiple directions for further development of this technique. With its potential to advance the understanding of multiphase flow design, this technique can contribute to field applications such as thermal management and material growth control. As a result, this work is expected to have a significant impact on research in these areas. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/edgarpot/skeletton.py. This approach allows us to leverage globally acquired skills and refine them with limited local data to identify road hazards in unfamiliar areas with minimal manual labels. Humans can learn to replicate complex movements with minimal instruction by observing others.  This capability is fundamental to imitation learning (IL), a field that aims to develop algorithms that can perform this task.  Most current IL algorithms are tailored to work within a specific context, generating movements that are similar to those observed.  They are not designed to transfer between different task settings, which typically require adjustments to movement patterns.  This study investigates a more general imitation problem where a novel task involves similar physics and dynamics but differs in terms of movement patterns.  We refer to this as a cross-area imitation problem.  To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel training approach that allows an agent to generate task-appropriate movements of varying lengths using offline pre-recorded data.  Our method involves constructing a latent representation of motion dynamics from observed trajectories and demonstrating the ability to generate diverse movements of different lengths.  We tested our approach on multiple complex simulators and found that it enables efficient learning of diverse movements between different task settings.  Additionally, our method allows an agent to generate diverse movements of different lengths in response to unseen inputs, exhibiting benefits in terms of demonstration length and the diversity of observed motions.  We compare our approach with established IL baselines and find that it outperforms them significantly.  Our findings suggest that imitation learning algorithms designed for cross-domain applications can facilitate efficient learning of diverse movements between different task settings. When inmates are released after serving time in prison, they face considerable obstacles that impede their ability to integrate into society.  Two key factors contributing to these challenges are the mental health issues that led to their incarceration and the lack of necessary treatment during their prison stint.  The aim of this study is to investigate the effect of mandated therapy for both sentenced and incarcerated individuals on their mental health.  Utilizing a cohort study based on data from Florida's prison system, the analysis identified the impact of required therapy on convicted individuals.  The results reveal that while necessary therapy had a positive effect on the mental health of the general population, it had a negative impact on those involved in the criminal justice system.  Furthermore, we investigate the reasons for this adverse reaction, focusing on the interaction between therapy and incarceration.  The relevant data indicates that incarceration can result in stigma, forcing individuals to conceal their treatment, thereby preventing it from having a positive effect.  The findings also suggest that incarceration can result in incarceration-related mental health issues.  Consequently, incarcerated individuals may benefit from alternative forms of treatment that take into account their distinct health requirements.  Additionally, we propose an alternative rationale for the adverse effect, suggesting that incarcerated individuals may be more susceptible to unfavorable therapy results due to ongoing societal factors.  Therefore, providing adequate support and services both during and after incarceration is vital to promote better mental health outcomes in this population.  While therapy may be beneficial for those convicted of crimes, its effectiveness depends on various variables, such as how it is delivered and who receives it.  More research is needed to understand these dynamics, as well as the underlying reasons for the adverse effect, in order to develop more effective mental health strategies that take into account the unique characteristics and experiences of those involved in the criminal justice system.  Furthermore, we highlight several potential avenues for further inquiry. In protoplanetary disks, carbon monoxide (CO) depletion serves as a marker for gas evaporation from icy particles, especially when comparing CO's radial abundance fluctuations in sub-millimeter continuum maps to its deuterated counterpart. The CO abundance decline in the AS 209 disk around a T Tauri star has been extensively examined in the Molecules with ALMA at Planetcreating Scales (MAPS) project. We analyze AS 209's CO emission patterns and CO--$^{13}$C emission data from the ALMA project to study this phenomenon. We use a radiative transfer model to explore the observed CO emission and its isotopes' spatial distribution. We find that CO's spatial structure in this disk features a double-peaked pattern at a 10 au scale, particularly in its CO--$^{13}$C emission map, with a minimum gap width of ~30 au at a 20% of $L_{\ast}$ intensity. This CO--$^{13}$C emission pattern is consistent with a model of chemical alteration, as it generates bimodal distributions of CO--$^{13}$C for certain inner disk radians. However, the overall CO depletion in this disk cannot be entirely attributed to a simple Thomson thin inner gaseous disk resulting from CO processing. We use a 2D gas dynamics model to explore the effect of a low-mass ('neo-classical' 0.015 $M_{\earth}$) photoevaporative flow originating from the disk's inner 0.1 AU radius and discover that it can explain 50% of CO depletion in this AS 209 case. Consequently, the overall CO depletion in this AS 209 disk likely results from a combination of gas evaporation and chemical alteration. Moreover, the overall depletion pattern of CO in AS 209 bears a striking resemblance to that of another star, CS 30312.2, examined in the MAPS project, suggesting common trends among evolved protoplanetary disks. These trends may imply that 'neo-classical' photoevaporation is a widespread phenomenon in disks devoid of massive inner holes. On the other hand, the 'high-mass' photoevaporation model failed to adequately explain CO depletion in this AS 209 case, as it produced a spotty, diffuse emission pattern at a 10 au scale, in direct contradiction with MAPS observations. We hypothesize that inner gaseous structures may be unstable and subject to rapid changes, as seen in recent sub-mm continuum images of AS 209

A flexible fracture emerges in rafts when they are subjected to high levels of stretch, causing the material to divide into distinct islands. This phenomenon is most prevalent in rafts composed of soft, elastic particles such as silicone beads, covering a broad spectrum of strain rates – from slow and manual manipulation to the high velocities induced by turbulence. As a result, understanding the behavior and accuracy of predicting raft fracture becomes increasingly important for applications involving the use of soft and flexible materials. This article aims to enhance current knowledge of fracture by providing a comprehensive analysis of its occurrence, along with the introduction of a novel theoretical model that explains the material's breakage from multiple aspects. Additionally, we examine the effects of particle softness on fracture through detailed simulations, revealing how the material's breakage changes under different levels of strain for stiffer particles, while presenting an new approach for designing more robust and flexible materials. Our findings also open the door for further research on fracture, along with promising avenues for future applications and investigations. It's also worth mentioning that our work doesn't cover biological systems such as living tissues, as we specifically focus on the fracture of soft and elastic materials. Our study does, however, shed light on new paths for further research on both biological systems and other types of elastic materials. Finally, we explore potential ways to apply our knowledge to practical problems, such as improving material durability by learning from our findings on particle softness and its impact on fracture. Our work is complemented by an online repository containing additional data and code needed to replicate our results and build upon our research. This includes numerical models used to simulate and study the material's breakage, along with experimental methods for observing and analyzing raft fracture. This extra information can serve as a valuable resource for future research and collaborations, further enhancing our understanding of fracture and flexible materials. We hope our study contributes to a deeper knowledge of soft and elastic materials, while inspiring new research and applications. Our work is specifically tailored to inspire theoretical and experimental contributions, rather than duplicating existing research. This includes promoting novel design strategies for improving material robustness, while identifying areas for further collaboration and investigation. This new information can potentially lead to breakthroughs in various fields such as materials science, biology, and aerodynamics, among others. Moreover, our work increases the likelihood of these advances by providing the necessary tools and a thorough analysis that sheds light on the complex phenomenon of raft fracture. This includes a detailed understanding of fracture's occurrence and new metrics for measuring material breakage. We hope our research will facilitate new developments and applications

In recent years, link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) has gained significant research attention.  To address this challenge, most existing approaches focus on incorporating temporal dimensions into knowledge graph representation learning (KGRL) models.  Contrary to traditional graph embedding techniques that rely on iterative training, some proposed methods utilize static framework models by leveraging large-scale pre-trained models.  This study investigates the feasibility of applying static framework models to link prediction in TKGs.  To achieve this, two novel methods, namely StaticFW and StaticFWC, are developed.  StaticFW employs a two-stage approach using pre-trained models from the HAKE framework, while StaticFWC builds upon the FeHAKE model by using a pre-trained continuous entity dictionary.  Experimental results on three large TKG datasets demonstrate the efficacy of StaticFW and StaticFWC in outperforming existing methods on line forecasting and knowledge graph completion metrics.  Notably, StaticFWC achieves superior performance with reduced computational complexity, making it a more efficient approach for large-scale TKGs.  Furthermore, a computational analysis and a model interpretability study on TheScapeFeHAKE validate the viability of using static framework models in link prediction.  Specifically, scaling TheScapeFeHAKE models through the number of entities yields linearly related MAP scores and a comparable level of accuracy to iterative training methods.  Furthermore, attributing the choices of incorrect entity predictions to their corresponding ground truth can effectively diagnose and alleviate errors.  To facilitate future research, the proposed methods, along with the generated knowledge graphs and evaluation code, are made available on an online repository.  Experimental results reveal that static framework models can effectively tackle the link prediction challenge in TKGs, offering efficient and scalable solutions.  These findings stem from models' robust generalization capabilities on knowledge graph representation learning and their ability to employ static embedding frameworks.  Notably, static framework models can leverage temporal information and employ distance hard mining without undergoing iterative training, thus supporting the research community in accurately modeling temporal contexts.  Furthermore, the employed static framework models and proposed methods demonstrate comparable performance on existing datasets, thus validating their viability and facilitating the reproduction of experimental results.  To showcase this, the online repository contains reproducible code and the generated knowledge graphs for rigorous testing.  These findings can be utilized by the knowledge graph embedding community to develop new and innovative approaches using static framework models for link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs. Identifying the atomic Rydberg states via optical transitions is challenging due to their low optical accessibility. Alternately, using external radiation sources like microwaves can facilitate detection, but this approach poses difficulties in achieving sufficient sensitivity. We have developed a new method that leverages multifrequency microwave radiation to detect Rydberg states with high precision. This innovative technique involves modeling Rabi oscillations using a deep neural network that incorporates multiple frequencies, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately predicting Rydberg state probabilities. Furthermore, our method enables the extraction of key energy level coupling parameters, specifically Rabi frequencies and Stark shifts, thereby facilitating high-precision quantum control. We have successfully tested this technique in an experiment involving $^{40}$Rb atoms, demonstrating a $10^4$ enhancement in the sensitivity of detecting Rydberg states based on microwave mediation. This highly sensitive detection method could greatly aid the development of high precision quantum computing and quantum network applications. Additionally, our deep learning approach can be adapted to detect Rydberg states in diverse atomic species and may contribute to the exploration of quantum phenomena in diverse systems. We have released the trained models and relevant software tools for this purpose, making this technology accessible to the scientific community. Bill Thurston initially found that the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure on a given three-manifold cannot drop below a certain lower limit. Subsequent work by David Gabai and David Meyer discovered that there is a similar lower limit for the Euler characteristic of transverse singularities in three-manifolds. David Cooper and David Long later proved that the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure on a three-manifold cannot be greater than a upper limit. We present here a new proof that combines these earlier results of Cooper and Long with further findings of Daniel Mathieu, establishing that the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure on a three-manifold satisfies a specific inequality. The relationship between the Euler characteristic of a tight contact structure and the Thurston norm supports this inequality. The proof relies on an analysis of the intersection forms associated with three-manifolds, as well as previously published records of the Euler characteristic of tight contact structures. A key obstacle in allowing humans to operate complex robots lies in bridging the gap between the human body's diverse movement patterns and the robot's movement vocabulary. Current solutions rely on data-driven approaches that learn and generate movement options for tasks, but these are limited by requirements of vast task datasets and precise task identification. We've developed a new task-independent technique that adapts a prelearned movement strategy to a new task by observing a human in action. This method, grounded in information theory, builds a task-specific movement framework by combining observed human movements and pretraining data. We achieve this through the use of a nonparametric movement representation and optimization algorithms that preserve structural characteristics. To demonstrate our approach's effectiveness, we designed an artificial task and tested it on human-robot collaboration, resulting in successful application to a Cobot-assisted packaging demonstration. In addition, we've expanded the movement strategy's utility to aid humans in recovering task-specific movement patterns from degraded or incomplete human motion data, common in robot-to-human collaboration. We've tested this in a variety of situations, including the interpretation of human shoulder movements in a packaging task and the recovery of drawing motions from partially recorded arm movements. These achievements mark the first time, to our knowledge, that information-theoretic methods have been combined with geometric transport techniques to tackle the operational challenges of human-robot collaboration, particularly in tasks like packaging and drawing. These successes have also been reflected in awards from the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, including the Best Applied Robotics Award and the Humanitarian Action Award. A new task titled 'Unintentional Turntables' is presented, focusing on training a camera perspective transformation model using unstructured, unrestrained video and three-dimensional object views. The task simulates real-world situations where students may accidentally spin objects while learning three-dimensional shapes through tactile exploration. By leveraging these spontaneously recorded videos, a monocular model can automatically adjust to rotate with the moving object and adapt to new views. The 'Unintentional Turntables' dataset was created to support this research and serves as a novel, extensive dataset containing diverse, unrestrained 3D object transformations. The approach to solving this task involves developing a novel raw video normalization technique, which removes redundant spatial and temporal information, and enables the model to concentrate on identifying the object's underlying shape. The results show that normalizing the video stream resolves the domain shift issue and enables effective shape transfer learning. Furthermore, by incorporating a novel three-dimensional shape prediction goal in addition to pose estimation, a 'ShapeTurntable' dual-objective model can be developed to tackle the task, significantly enhancing performance. The code and dataset are publicly available for testing and study purposes. The approach to solving this task can be utilized in various scenarios where agents may encounter and transform objects, and can be adapted to strengthen self-driving vehicle capability in challenging situations. Due to the contagious nature of social media, misinformation about COVID-19 has spread rapidly, leading to widespread concerns about its consequences. The primary obstacle in managing social media misinformation is encouraging people to truthfully express their past experiences of encountering false information. To overcome this challenge, we developed an innovative approach called TwieeNet, a neural network that identifies dialogue participants' past experiences with misinformation on COVID-19 vaccines. In particular, TwieeNet was trained to determine whether a user in a Twitter conversation accepts or rejects vaccine-related misinformation based on the content of user posts. Using a labeled dataset consisting of 3,599 annotated dialogues, we demonstrated the efficacy of our approach by achieving a performance score of 84.4% for message classification and 81.9% for message ranking. Notably, TwieeNet performed accept/rejection tasks more efficiently compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, while also showcasing its capacity for adapting to task variations and accommodating different encoding strategies. Finally, case studies were conducted to illustrate the practical applications and ethical considerations of our approach. Source code for this project is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jbtxie/TwieeNet. Additionally, the demo video can be found at https://youtu.be/yP29gM_3T4U. Experimental findings and data visualizations are available at https://cse.mnnu.edu.tw/~jbtse/TwieeNet. The production and control of high-energy attosecond pulses, lasting only a few hundred attoseconds, hold significant potential for advancing the field of attosecond science. These pulses enable precise measurement of electronic processes within molecules and matter, leading to a deeper understanding of their behavior. To further the development of attosecond science, we must overcome two main challenges: achieving higher pulse energies while maintaining short pulse durations. Our work focuses on addressing this issue by demonstrating a novel scheme that produces high-energy attosecond pulses coherently, using the interaction of two laser fields with an argon atom. Our approach leverages the robustness of a crucial physical phenomenon, making it insensitive to critical parameters that typically influence attosecond pulse generation, such as ionization, charge recursion, and energy drift. Additionally, we demonstrate that our scheme can produce pulses with energies of hundreds of electronvolts and demonstrate the feasibility of manipulating coherent attosecond pulse pairs using controlled laser fields, opening up new avenues for the advancement of attosecond science and laser-matter interaction research. The implementation of our scheme using table-top laser technology holds considerable promise for the development of new applications in both laboratory and real-world settings. Our findings indicate that coherent pulse manipulation could serve as a fundamental paradigm for achieving high-energy attosecond pulses in various physical contexts. Furthermore, we anticipate that our research will stimulate a broader exploration of new ideas in the field of coherent attosecond pulse generation. The combined potential of our scheme, along with cutting-edge X-ray free-electron lasers and next-generation Higgs boson facility, holds great promise for the future of attosecond science. Our study offers a fundamental contribution to coherent pulse manipulation and attosecond pulse generation, along with concrete numerical evidence and colorful two-dimensional visualizations to support our findings, which are available at arxiv.org/abs/2003.006792. For a stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation with pure jump noise and random initial conditions, we demonstrate that irreducibility is preserved regardless of the perturbation strength. We also examine the sufficiency and necessity of conditions for irreducibility in two specific cases, providing necessary and sufficient conditions in one scenario and insufficient but plausible conditions in another. These findings are supported by two distinct examples. Additionally, we investigate the long-term properties of the solution's probability density function and its relation to a stationary measure. These results are accompanied by graphical representations of the solutions' behavior for various values of the perturbation strength. We begin by reviewing the key concepts and tools required for the subsequent analysis. We then establish the preservation of irreducibility and provide an initial assessment of the sufficiency of conditions for irreducibility. Following this, we delve into the precise examination of the sufficiency of conditions for irreducibility, followed by the presentation of two illustrative examples. Finally, we conclude by analyzing the long-term properties of the solution. Our work is motivated by the applications of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations in modeling various physical phenomena, such as superfluids and superconductors, as well as our prior study on the irreducibility of stochastic real Ginzburg-Landau equations and its related mathematical models. Diffusion is a fundamental concept that underlies many scientific and engineering applications. Although it may seem straightforward, the process of interest diffusion in many fields can be quite complex and often lacks a clear definition. Furthermore, solving these diffusion-based problems can be very challenging. To tackle this issue, a novel approach using a weighted average of past values and incremental updates has been developed. This method, called the Fractional Countermeasures (FCm) approach, is capable of modeling a wide range of diffusions, including stochastic and deterministic forms. By leveraging its inherent properties, such as time-irreversibility and non-locality, the FCm approach can facilitate novel numerical schemes that are both efficient and accurate. To demonstrate its efficacy, numerical experiments have been conducted to verify the development of a new numerical lender and its applicability to diverse diffusion models. Moreover, the FCm approach has been successfully applied to real-world problems, such as simulating the spread of COVID-19 and modeling temperature variations. The results show that the FCm method can be an effective tool for solving numerical diffusion problems and has great potential for future use. The study's findings are expected to be very helpful. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing properties at the nanoscale. The profile of spin density in these materials exhibits remarkable local variations that are fundamentally linked to the concepts of chirality and structural asymmetry. Using a full-potential method based on the DMFT approach, we thoroughly investigate the effects of asymmetry and chiral interactions on the spin density in the CrI$_3$ bilayer, which significantly differs from the ideal crystal structure due to van der Waals gaps. Our studies reveal the presence of pronounced inter-layer asymmetry in spin density and demonstrate that chiral interactions induce noticeable magnetic polarizations across the bilayer junction. Interestingly, we find that van der Waals gaps do not necessarily give rise to distinct magnetic regions within the bilayer, as the spin and valley states remain strongly coupled across the bilayer in the CrI$_3$ bilayer setting. Our research, however, reveals that this coupling does not significantly affect the Rashba-type effect in this context. Our findings provide comprehensive insights into the relationship between chirality, Rashba effect, and asymmetry in 2D magnetic semiconductors, as seen in CrI$_3$ bilayers. Furthermore, we suggest that experimentally inducing chiral interactions could significantly modulate the optical properties of these materials by altering the profile of spin and valley states. Our study opens up new avenues for exploring asymmetry and chiral interactions in 2D magnetic semiconductors and their impact on the material's optical properties. We've developed a new class of inflationary models, incorporating locally supersymmetric "efficient field theories." These models build upon previous work, expanding the concept of efficient fields, which originaly incorporated a dust-like matter field, then generalized to a cosmic fluid with multiple degrees of freedom, and most recently, introduced a cosmic fluid with non-geodesic motion. Our new model encompasses the time derivative of the efficient field as an additional degree of freedom, and due to PSF constraints, this time derivative behaves like a cosmic fluid with pressure and energy density proportional to the tensor prepotential. Our locally supersymmetric efficient field theory of inflationary cosmology specifically incorporates two degrees of freedom: a scalar field and a pseudoscalar field, both related to the prepotential. The scalar field corresponds to the Hubble scale of the universe, while the pseudoscalar field is closely tied to the de Sitter metric, and both fields are bound together by a supersymmetric relationship. Our model features a unique characteristic solutions: a scalar prepotential, a pseudoscalar axion field, and a supersymmetric partner fermion field. This study analyzes how COVID-19 news coverage across 90 U.S. metropolitan areas relates to local infection and death rates, audience size, and newspaper profitability. Our results show that areas with higher COVID coverage received more resources from the federal government, suggesting a link between media attention and public health investment. Interestingly, the death toll in covered cities exceeded those with less COVID reporting, which may indicate a delay in media response to local COVID crises. Our data also suggest that smaller, non-daily newspapers, serving smaller populations, were more likely to increase COVID coverage as the pandemic worsened, while larger newspapers, serving bigger populations, showed less variation in COVID coverage trends. Ultimately, areas with more COVID coverage saw higher death rates, yet both news cycles and mortality rates were unaffected by the local audience size. Our findings imply that the amount of COVID coverage in the U.S. was not enough to prevent the pandemic's devastating consequences but may have influenced public health investment and policy decisions. Like non-daily newspapers, big dailies initially underreported the pandemic, only ramping up coverage after the crisis had peaked and spread widely across the country, which may indicate a common reliance on official sources and delayed critical examination of government policies during the early stages of the pandemic. This method leverages gradients derived from image progress not used for prediction, enabling our agent to achieve a high degree of accuracy in actual navigation tasks. Ultimately, our strategy provides a strategy with minimal memory requirements that can successfully navigate new environments in actual worlds. The interface between europium sulfide and indium arsenide has drawn attention due to its potential to produce a precise magnetic field in a two-dimensional system, which has significant applications including the observation of magnetoelectric effects and flat band phenomena. There is a lack of consensus among different computational studies on the electronic properties at the EuS/InAs interface. To resolve these discrepancies, we conducted a highly accurate study of the electronic properties at the interface, utilizing a stable crystal structure obtained through a minimally invasive atomic relaxation process, and found that the electronic properties significantly depend on the chemical bonds between the two materials, which vary based on the specific bonding arrangement. Our results demonstrate that the electronic properties are inappropriate when the interface consists of mismatched materials and incorrect bond lengths are used. Conversely, when the correct bonds are formed, the electronic properties correctly represent the charge distribution, and our findings are consistent with experiments. We found that the electronic energy loss and dielectric response are significantly influenced by the breakdown of symmetry at the interface, particularly in the case of asymmetrical bonding arrangements. Additionally, we observed a significant shift in transition charge density and self-energy at the interface in aspherical bonding arrangements. Our study is the most accurate investigation of the electronic properties at the EuS/InAs interface, and we predict distinct features in the reflectivity and absorption spectra of InAs that can be experimentally validated. The complexity of deep learning models continues to outpace the capacity of current computing infrastructure, hindering deployment on resource-constrained devices.  A promising approach to mitigating this issue is model pruning, which enables the removal of redundant components from the model without sacrificing accuracy.  While existing pruning methods primarily focus on generalization to unseen data, they often result in significant function loss and inefficiencies when applied to existing models.  This paper introduces ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end training framework combining the benefits of both traditional and progressive pruning methods.  Unlike existing approaches that only consider the model's structure, ClickTrain comprehensively evaluates both the models and their training processes, and leverages this information to adapt and fine-tune pruned models through a series of iterative re-training cycles.  The framework undergoes extensive evaluation on widely-used datasets, and our results reveal that ClickTrain can effectively and efficiently remove up to 99.5% of model parameters with minimal accuracy loss, and even outperforms state-of-the-art methods when a small amount of data is available for training.  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghaofeiyang/ClickTrain.  Evaluation results may be accessed through https://clicktrain.com/.  Future research directions are also provided.  Overall, ClickTrain offers a pioneering approach to model pruning and re-training, and can serve as a reliable foundation for future work in this domain.  Although specific performance may vary depending on the specific pruned models used, our general findings and observations are universally applicable.  Our experiments are repeatable, and our source code is publicly accessible, enabling anyone to reproduce our results and replicate our research. We develop a novel primal-dual algorithm to solve complex Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with constraints that vary over time. In these scenario-based MDPs, certain rules must be adhered to at specific time intervals within the episode duration. Our approach adapts the primal-dual technique to address time-dependent constraints in MDPs, yielding a substantial reduction in computational complexity. Specifically, it results in a $O(T^{2.5} \sqrt{D})$ time complexity using $O(\sqrt{T})$ iterations, where $D$ represents the diameter of the state space, which improves existing methods requiring $T^{3.5}$ operations. Additionally, we investigate the performance guarantees for obtaining optimal reward-to-go functions, providing a framework for future research to achieve optimal policies. Our proposed method is accompanied by a detailed mathematical proof and demonstrated in numerical experiments involving various constraint patterns, including 1) time-dependent thresholds, 2) state-action constraint violation, and 3) exponential violation thresholds. The results showcase our method's superiority to alternative methods across different scenarios. Furthermore, we examine how our approach can be modified to solve online learning problems with sequential arrival of instances, resulting in a $O(T^{1.25} \sqrt{\log T} \log T)$ time complexity. Our primal-dual method displays a superior performance in reward maximization experiments on real-world datasets when compared to other competing methods. The code and additional findings are accessible online at the specified repository.

Presence-absence data represents species occurrence at particular locations with yes/no values, which is a type of binary matrix that needs to be analyzed for community ecology research. This study investigates the effectiveness of eight clustering methods, including information theoretic, model-based, and hierarchical approaches, all applied to simulated and real datasets from the Biodiversity Evaluation and Information Management Department of Brazil's Wildlife Conservation. Our results reveal that the BT clustering method along with OT clustering show promise for ecological studies, particularly when dealing with difficult-to-interpret simulated data, while being relatively unsuitable for real-life species data despite performing well in both cases in terms of sililarity. Our code is publicly accessible through the presenceabsence cluster package in R.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, particularly GPUs, has become indispensable for scientific and engineering simulations, making object-oriented programming on these systems a pressing research need. Despite significant advancements, object-oriented memory management on GPUs still relies heavily on manual memory allocation, which is both prone to memory leaks and difficult to manage. To address these challenges, we have developed DynaSOAr, a novel concurrent memory allocator for object-oriented programming on GPUs, incorporating a dynamic memory allocation system, a data structure for tracking memory usage, and a collision hash table for efficient data access. By combining these components, DynaSOAr offers superior memory management, including automatic memory allocation and deallocation, rapid memory access, and simultaneous access to shared memory without conflicts. Experimental results demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, including manual memory allocation, MMAP, and BMAM, resulting in a substantial speedup of 3.97 times and significant memory usage reductions of up to 97.69%. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's accurate memory management also helps to significantly reduce memory leaks by as much as 99.97%. These breakthroughs enable DynaSOAr to effectively support high-benefit factors for an industrial-scale application, including real-time ray tracing, object tracking, and memory access optimization. The work presents a new approach to concurrent memory management, showcasing DynaSOAr's potential applications in various domains. The findings indicate that with the application of external pressure, the stress patterns in the conduit become more complex than initially anticipated, particularly near the closed end of the conduit, where the stress patterns differ significantly from those experienced by cylindrical structures. Furthermore, the results reveal that the strains experienced by the conduit due to external pressure are not sufficient to induce plastic deformation. The findings also indicate that the magnitude of deformation experienced by the inner wall of the conduit is directly proportional to the pressure levels applied in the simulation. However, uneven skin pigmentation can distort the accuracy of diagnostic outcomes. Recent research employs machine learning models, specifically neural networks, to minimize these errors. Although these models perform well, they often struggle with identifying unusual patterns in data. This study introduces a novel algorithm that utilizes entropy to pinpoint outlier samples and enhances a deep learning model's accuracy in identifying skin lesions. By integrating this method into the training process, we can optimize a deep learning model for detecting skin lesions. Furthermore, reducing data anomalies through anomaly removal increased the accuracy of the model, while outlier removal decreased the model's accuracy. This suggests that unusual data has a negative impact on the accuracy of the model, which can be mitigated by removing such data. Our proposed algorithm utilizes entropy to identify and remove unusual data, thereby improving the accuracy of the model. We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from almost-free electron model predictions. These predictions state that the mass enhancement factor increases linearly with the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf{q}$ from the Fermi surface to the momentum where the photoelectron is emitted. To resolve the discrepancy, we modeled sodium as a simple tight-binding electron in a one-dimensional lattice and calculated the mass enhancement factor as a function of $\mathbf{q}$ using both weak scattering and strong scattering models. The results revealed that the strength of electron-phonon interactions and the number of nearest neighbor scattering paths available to quasiparticles significantly limit the linear increase of mass enhancement factor, especially in the case of two-nearest-neighbor scattering. Consequently, the lifetime of quasiparticles in real sodium is significantly shorter than predicted, leading to a non-linear increase in the mass enhancement factor as a function of $\mathbf{q}$. Our findings provide a framework for future researchers to test our model and conduct similar studies on other electron-phonon coupled systems. Additionally, the proposed experimental protocol could be used to measure the impact of additional mechanisms, such as electron-electron interactions, that may be significant in other materials like lead. Unfortunately, existing methods often result in unrecoverable distortions due to their use of non-reversible transformation functions, which severely limits their practical applications. To address this issue, this study introduces a novel framework called Reversible Concealment Framework (RCF) aimed at developing reversible concealment methods. The proposed RCF comprises two primary components: a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) model and an optimization module. To simulate finding adversarial examples, we developed an optimization module that maximizes image noise while ensuring the network's prediction remains unchanged. The study presents extensive experimental evidence confirming that the proposed RCF provides a reliable means of generating reversible adversarial examples, which can be utilized for various purposes such as data compression, feature extraction, and testing the robustness of neural networks. Recent studies have shown that humans use local and regional movement patterns in their heads when identifying objects, a discovery that has potential implications for the development of advanced robotic and computer systems with object recognition abilities. For example, in a scenario where a person is identifying a cup, the individual may focus on the overall shape of the cup to determine its boundaries, while also using local characteristics such as the cup's handle to gather further information. This process can be thought of as using both local and regional cues to achieve accurate identification. Although this discovery has far-reaching implications for various fields, there have been few attempts so far to incorporate it into dynamic object recognition models. This paper presents a new approach called the Local and Regional Cues (LRC) model, which combines both local and regional movement patterns in its decision-making process. The model's performance has been compared to that of existing object recognition models, including a bi-directional Gated Recurrent Unit (BRGRU) model, using a dataset of human motor cortex activity associated with object identification in the Minimal Clip dataset. Our analysis of the results shows that the LRC model outperforms the BRGRU model in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, while also offering a simpler and more interpretable solution. In brain tissue, the balance of nutrients and waste products relies heavily on a complex system of substance transport across the blood-brain barrier and through the brain tissue itself. To maintain proper nutrient and waste removal, the substance transport system must be highly regulated - delivering necessary nutrients and limiting the entry of toxic substances to cells. Unfortunately, the accurate modeling of this process is hindered by a lack of detailed information about the underlying biology, forcing researchers to make various assumptions. One potential approach to developing substance transport models is the use of PDE-constrained optimization, a method which can be used to model the substance transport system as a whole and also account for the biological processes that regulate it.

We present a new model for substance transport regulation, based on a optimization problem that incorporates partial differential equations, and divide it into two distinct components: first we must determine how the substance transport system should be configured to meet a certain objective, and then we must select the appropriate parameters to implement this configuration. To solve this problem, we develop novel methods for evaluating the desirability of different substance transport configurations and for using this information to set optimal parameter values. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and its ability to capture key features of the substance transport system.

One of the primary challenges in developing substance transport models is the varying effectiveness of different substance transport mechanisms, which can transport nutrients, waste products, and signals across cell membranes. How to model the regulation of these mechanisms, given limited information about their role in the substance transport system? We present a set of continuous optimization problems that enforce the biological plausibility of different substance transport configurations, and use these problems to develop new model adaptation methods. These optimization problems ensure that substance transport mechanisms only work as signal receivers or signal producers when it makes biological sense, and when it comes to nutrient transport, the models ensure that substance transport mechanisms work only when nutrients are present in the surroundings. 

Another issue in developing substance transport models is the role of different substance transport mechanisms in the substance transport system. How to model this role, given limited information about it? We present a set of discrete optimization problems that enforce the biological plausibility of different substance transport configurations, and use these problems to develop new model adaptation methods. These optimization problems balance the role of different substance transport mechanisms in the substance transport system by taking into account their relative importance. 

We present numerical simulations that demonstrate our ability to develop biologically plausibly substance transport models using optimization techniques and our ability to make these models adaptable to different situations using constraint theory.

A broad group of Tversky metrics is defined by a straightforward formula that allows for the calculation of diverse distance measures between crisp sets. By adjusting the parameters in this formula, the Jaccard distance and a variant of the normalized information distance that was introduced earlier by Mihelich and Wang can be obtained. This demonstrates that the Jaccard distance is a limiting case of the Tversky metric, while the variant of the normalized information distance is a specific instance of it, known as the normalized generalized information distance. We examine the properties of the generalized Jaccard distance and its reverse, the generalized similarity measure, as well as their invariance with respect to both matrix and set operations. Furthermore, the stability analysis for both the Jaccard distance and the normalized generalized information distance reveals that they are highly stable under different uncertainty models that affect their parameters. Nonetheless, only one particular case yields perfectly stable results: this occurs when both parameters equal 1/2, resulting in the traditional generalized information distance, which was previously found to be highly stable. We also provide a geometric interpretation that explains how the Jaccard distance, the normalized generalized information distance, and their reverse counterparts behave in relation to the random uncertainty model. In addition, a numerical example highlights the practical differences in the predictions made by the Jaccard distance, the normalized generalized information distance, and their reverse counterparts for two arbitrary sets, demonstrating that these predictions can be misleading when both set membership and non-membership are uncertain. A conclusion summarizes the key findings and highlights their practical implications. We also offer some suggestions for future research. What is more, two new metrics are suggested here that can replace the normalized generalized information distance in a previous study by combining the Jaccard distance with both set membership and non-membership degrees. These two metrics are found to be effective in addressing the issues raised in the aforementioned example, while their stability under different uncertainty models is also analyzed through both theoretical and numerical methods. Ultimately, we examine the relationship between entropy and divergence, and apply this study to define a new set difference operation, called the divergent difference, between two arbitrary sets, along with a method for computing it easily. Furthermore, we extend our approach to the case of fuzzy sets by generalizing the Jaccard distance, the normalized generalized information distance, and their reverse counterparts for fuzzy sets, and also investigate their stability under different uncertainty models for fuzzy sets, along with a geometric interpretation through V-dictionary sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the equivalence between specifying a complete extended real array $X$ and defining a saturated arrangement $\mathcal{R}$ on this set, and we use this result to establish two distinct characterizations of when an arranged set $X$ is complete. First, we show that each set in a covering $\{X_i\}$ of $X$ must be complete. Conversely, if each set in a covering $\{X_i\}$ of $X$ is complete, then $X$ is complete. Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every complete graph of size n can be colored with n colors such that any subset of n-1 vertices uses the same color. This would imply that n-1 vertices can contain every possible edge. This study confirms that complete graphs of size 4 and 5 meet this criterion, whereas earlier work established the same for 3-colorable networks. To achieve this result, a list-coloring approach was used to show that every 4-set or 5-set of vertices in these complete graphs can form every possible edge combination. This led to the formulation of two new hypotheses that may aid in resolving the broader Hadwiger's Conjecture. This approach also allowed for the creation of a more straightforward proof of a 1972 theorem by Erdos, Sparlund, and Tuza, which demonstrated that complete graphs of size n can be colored with n-1 colors such that any subset of n-2 vertices uses the same color. Furthermore, this study confirmed the converse of another 1972 theorem and provided an alternate proof of another result stated in the Duke Mathematics Journal. This work will lead to the publication of a separate paper containing further findings and proofs related to this topic. To overcome this challenge, the proposed method incorporates a kernel width optimization strategy, enabling the use of an orthogonal fixed-point algorithm to efficiently estimate the kernel width. As a result, the method can effectively minimize the mean squared error (MSE) while promoting the optimization of the kernel width. The proposed AGC-SGWKO method has been extensively evaluated using synthetic and real-world datasets, and our findings demonstrate its superior performance and robustness compared to other graph signal recovery methods. The computational complexity and memory requirements of the method were also analyzed, and our experimental results indicate that it outperforms existing methods while requiring significantly lower computational resources and memory. The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) is a simplified model that combines active movement and random movement from thermal motion. By introducing a linear feedback mechanism, the AOUP captures the non-linear dynamics of many active movement systems. Our investigation focused on the behavior of multiple AOUPs in a confined space with a single chemical gradient present, revealing two distinct states - either persistent motion towards the gradient source or stationary movement around the gradient. We demonstrated that one persistent state corresponds to a global minimum of a defined function, while the other stationary state is a saddle point. Furthermore, our analysis uncovered two distinct timescales associated with the persistent state, influencing the motion: a rapid movement towards the gradient and a slower drifting movement around the gradient. Our findings were further validated through experimental observations of E. coli bacteria under similar conditions. We applied an analytical model to describe the persistent motion, taking into account variations in movement and chemical gradient properties. Our analysis suggests that rapid movement is primarily influenced by movement properties, while the speed of drifting movement around the gradient is determined by a combination of movement and chemical gradient properties. Furthermore, our study indicates that the persistence time is longer when the variance in movement is higher than the variance in response to the chemical gradient. We introduce HUMBI, a groundbreaking large-scale multiview dataset featuring human body gestures.  With over 109k video segments spanning multiple viewpoints, this collection is the largest of its kind.  Each video segment is approximately 10 seconds long and accompanied by a detailed annotation outlining the-grasp configuration in full detail.  The dataset was crafted from some of the most popular gaming accessories instructional videos on YouTube, making it diverse and rich in representation.  To facilitate advanced machine learning research, we developed three effective evaluation benchmarks for single-view, multiview, and low-light scenarios.  Additionally, we established the 'HUMBI Challenge' to drive progress in these areas, with the goal of attracting top researchers in the field.  We have successfully validated state-of-the-art approaches on our benchmark, and the 'HUMBI Challenge' is now open for competition.  You can access the dataset at https://humbi.github.io/.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, developments in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have long concentrated on English due to the difficulty and cost of collecting and labeling data in other languages. We introduce a novel approach to independent and universal model transfer across languages by leveraging neural task representations, which can be learned and used without requiring task-specific labels. Our method utilizes weak labels, and evaluates task similarity and lingual differences separately, allowing for a fine-grained control over cross-lingual transfer. We demonstrate our approach's effectiveness through successful transfer of NLP tasks across 10 languages, achieving state-of-the-art results on 4 sentiment analysis datasets, and achieving comparable results on 4 other datasets. Our method is model-independent, easy to use, and requires minimal information about the target dataset. It also enables direct comparisons of lingual representations and can be applied to analyze the similarity and differences between languages. We make our code and trained models available to the public. With our approach, we believe that deep NLP models can be transferred more easily across languages, making high-quality NLP research more accessible and affordable. Our transfer model is a significant breakthrough, particularly for developing countries with limited resources, as it allows them to develop advanced NLP systems without having to spend a lot of money on data labeling. It also enables us to understand and analyze the similarities and differences between languages, which is crucial for many applications in linguistics and NLP. Our work is a significant contribution to the field of NLP, as it solves the long-standing problem of transferring models across languages, and makes widespread use of the English neural task representations' high quality. It also enables us to understand and analyze the similarities and differences between languages, and demonstrates that deep NLP models can be transferred effectively across languages. Our method is a flexible and general approach to independent and universal model transfer, and we believe that it can be applied successfully to a wide range of NLP tasks and datasets. We tested our approach on 10 languages, and it achieved state-of-the-art results on 8 datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our transfer model is also very efficient, as it requires minimal information about the target dataset. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by replacing the initial propagation and alignment modules with more advanced alternatives. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, consistently outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Our detailed analysis shows that the improved modules are responsible for this boost in performance by effectively incorporating information from the input video. Additionally, we have made the original BasicVSR code available to facilitate further research and comparisons. Our experimental results demonstrate the superiority of BasicVSR++ on a wide range of datasets and resolution levels, with a corresponding increase in efficiency due to a significant reduction in the number of modules and parameters. Specifically, BasicVSR++ surpasses the performance of the state-of-the-art models by a considerable margin, with a notable 5.64% improvement in PSNR for the intermediate scale of $720^2$, and is up to $3\times$ more efficient than the nearest rival. BasicVSR++ also consistently outperforms other top-performing models in video restoration tasks, such as video denoising and compression artifacts removal, with a notable improvement in PSNR of up to $4.0$ and $2.0$ respectively, and is about $2\times$ more efficient than the nearest rival in these tasks. Our research further validates the effectiveness of our enhanced model using alternative evaluation metrics, such as SSIM and MS-SSD, solidifying its superiority in video SR performance. Ultimately, BasicVSR++ sets a new standard in video super-resolution, achieving superior performance and efficiency across a range of resolutions and compression levels, and is suitable for various video enhancement tasks like denoising and compression artifacts removal. This method is compatible with a variety of learning algorithms, including deep learning and neural networks. Extreme weather events like hurricanes and storm surges have devastating impacts on power delivery systems, resulting in widespread outages that can leave millions of people without electricity. To investigate the effects of these events, a numerical model simulates the combination of storm surges and atmospheric conditions to generate detailed maps of wind and water levels down to 10 meters in depth. This information is then used to analyze the performance of power transmission lines by evaluating damage to infrastructure and computing outage rates for both linear and nonlinear systems. A study was conducted in the state of Florida to examine the spatial and temporal influence of storm surges on line losses and outage rates as they correlate with increasing water levels and wind speeds. Results indicate that both factors significantly contribute to the deterioration of power transmission, with surges resulting in significantly higher rates of damage and loss compared to storm-driven wind alone. This effect is observed across various line configurations and particularly pronounced in systems over 100 miles from the coast, where surge-related losses may outnumber those from wind. To further contribute to mitigation efforts, two potential strategies are proposed to strengthen the resilience of power infrastructure against storm surges, namely relocating or elevating transmission lines, which show promise in reducing outage rates and minimizing damage to infrastructure. This research provides valuable insights to grid operators and infrastructure planners alike on how to effectively prepare and manage power delivery systems in the face of storm-induced disruptions. This knowledge can be applied well beyond Florida, as relevant to any region susceptible to hurricanes and storm surges. Research efforts such as this one, enabled by advanced computational modeling and simulation tools, are crucial towards achieving smart and resilient energy infrastructure. The effect of storm surges on power transmission infrastructure needs to be thoroughly investigated to develop effective strategies in designing and managing such systems. Although this study was conducted under the specifications of Florida's energy infrastructure, the methodology can easily be applied elsewhere to investigate the impact of storm surges on power delivery systems in diverse geographical settings and under different weather conditions. This research offers an important contribution towards understanding the numerical approach of simulating storm surges and their effect on infrastructure and can potentially aid in similar studies involving different types of extreme weather events and their interaction with energy systems. The damage model used in this study, for example, also takes into account the influence of wind speeds, atmospheric pressure, and barometric pressure in generating detailed maps of wind and water levels down to 10 meters in depth, which in itself presents an valuable contribution towards understanding the spatial and temporal distribution of storm-induced wind and water levels in this context. A crucial application of this theorem is in entropy theory to identify unique stationary measures for which the Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees uniqueness, and this new measure is more informative than previous ones when system parameters change. However, this new measure may not be unique or approachable under certain conditions. To resolve ambiguity, we need to identify all stable solutions for a system, especially for the Heterochaos baker map, which has an infinite period and log polynomial growth. We demonstrate that these stable solutions form a set of disconnected areas, and unlike traditional entropy approaches, detailed analysis of each component is necessary to understand how they change periodically and why they fail to approach a single measure as a parameter varies. We've explored how similar scalar sectors in various beyond-the-Standard Model theories are set up and whether they can be detected at upcoming colliders such as the Future Circular Electron Positron Collider (FCC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). In specific, we examined the characteristics of scalar fields with lepton-flavour universality violation and naturalness-driven electroweak symmetry breaking with a heavy top partner. In each case, we established the necessary conditions for detecting additional scalars at colliders. Within the context of scalar sectors featuring flavour-dependent couplings, our study serves as a general framework that can be extended to other similar setups. In particular, we demonstrated how the flavour anatomy of an ordinary EW doublet model with bare coefficients, augmented by a second doublet with flavour-dependent couplings, could be probed through precise differential cross-section measurements of $Z$ boson production. This analysis highlights the significance of performing a thorough flavour analysis to fully explore the potential of future collider experiments. In the context of naturalness-driven electro-weak symmetry breaking with a heavy top partner, we showed that the parameter space of the model can be divided into distinct regions according to the mass splittings within different scalar multiplets. We established the boundaries of this partitioning, which corresponds to different production mechanisms of additional scalars at colliders, and found that the model's scalar sectors can be probed through complete momentum spectra of produced scalars. In total, our study has identified various detection possibilities for enhanced scalar sectors at upcoming colliders. Additionally, our analysis has emphasized the importance of examining the flavour structure of scalar spectra in order to fully explore the potential of future collider experiments. This work could serve as a general detection guide for similar scalar spectra in various beyond-the-Standard Model theories featuring flavour-dependent flavour anatomy. In particular, we have demonstrated how the flavour anatomy of an ordinary EW doublet model with flavour-dependent couplings of scalars, as well as the flavour anatomy of naturalness-driven electroweak symmetry breaking with a heavy top partner, can be probed through precise differential cross-section measurements of $Z$ boson production.
